title: IB English A: Language & Literature
description: Explore how literary and non-literary texts shape ideas about culture, identity and power, and how those influences shape language in turn. Develop your analysis through close reading of different text types.

items.title: Reading words and images
items.summary: How do textual and visual choices shape our response?
items.body:
## Our guiding question
How do verbal and visual choices shape our response?

## Read and notice
Bring a passage or image from your current class text. Make three observations about the choices its creator has made.

## Discuss
- Which detail most strongly shapes your response?
- How might another reader interpret it differently?
- What evidence helps you explain your reading?

## Make your thinking visible
Try the close reading lab, then use the paragraph workshop to turn one interpretation into a developed response.

items.title: From observation to analysis
items.summary: Connect evidence to meaning, with a worked example and interactive magic-sentence workshop.
items.body:
## Start with a precise observation
What word, image, pattern, or structural choice catches your attention? Quote briefly and accurately.

## Explore a possible effect
How might that choice shape a reader’s response? Consider the context before making a claim about its effect.

## Connect detail to meaning
Explain how the evidence supports your interpretation. A useful starting phrase is: “This choice suggests … because …”

## Test your interpretation
Can you find a second detail that supports your reading? Is there evidence that complicates it? Revise your idea if necessary.

items.title: Paper 1
items.summary: Analyze how verbal and visual choices in a previously unseen non-literary text create meaning.
items.body:
## Briefing

Paper 1 is a guided analysis of previously unseen non-literary material. The guiding question gives you a productive way into the text: use it to build a focused interpretation rather than attempting to catalog everything you notice.

SL students choose one of the two texts. HL students analyze both. In either case, the central job is the same: explain how deliberate choices shape meaning for a particular audience and purpose.

> **First principle:** establish what the text is doing as a whole before examining individual details. Technique only matters when it helps explain that larger purpose.

## Method

[Unpack the guiding question](/resources/unpacking-questions#paper-1) before selecting your evidence.


[Writing an introduction: step-by-step guidance and a worked example](/resources/paper-1-introductions?example=language-literature)

### 1. Orient

- Read the contextual information and identify the text type, creator, audience, purpose, and situation.
- Record your first response. What seems urgent, unsettling, persuasive, intimate, comic, or controlled?
- Read the guiding question closely. Put what it asks you to analyze into your own words.

### 2. Survey

- Divide the text into meaningful sections and note shifts in tone, argument, focus, scale, or visual emphasis.
- Identify the overall movement of the text before concentrating on isolated devices.
- For multimodal texts—those combining forms such as words and images—trace the relationship between words, image, layout, typography, framing, and sequence.
- If the text is an infographic, consult the [Infographic guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/c1e54cf5-1489-440b-a98c-3e7107bacc62) for questions about hierarchy, scale, labels and source.
- For commercial advertising, use the [Advertisement guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/cf482e4c-3555-4e12-afca-b63396aec3ea) and its separate FIJI Water example to examine appeals, product claims and visual contrast.

- For fundraising, use the [Charitable appeal guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/b0a0e8bb-7dfb-4fd6-8da0-a19d3dc95e92) and its Elephant Sanctuary and WWF examples to connect need, trust and participation.

- For drawn commentary, use the [Cartoons guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/64dc8a9a-f80c-4e62-8a60-55a641a7b7f7) and its Andy Singer example to connect text, image and panel arrangement.

- For online personal writing and advice, use the [Blog post guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/a6b9e918-4b25-4ae8-9f6c-08bd45c89173) and its Emberton example to connect voice, illustrations and the development of an argument.

- For arguments and columns, use the [Opinion/commentary guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/9860d817-e8b4-4a15-b499-b0df6b780f28) and its netball example to connect tone with the development of a position.

- For public addresses, use the [Speech guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/501e5fac-47a8-4c41-a081-ac57220685c2) and Helen Clark’s eulogy to connect language, occasion and audience.

- For reporting and explanation, use the [Articles guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/b773dc6e-4794-4c80-a99f-8cdd183b20f4) to connect an article’s angle, sources and language.

- For digital layout and routes through a page, use the [Webpages guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/81d752ad-9f14-43a5-a7b5-34e14a7a7803) and the Redwoods Treewalk example.

- For addressed writing, use the [Letters guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/027cb949-724f-4872-bef8-4f2599684139) to connect purpose, recipient and relationship.

- For spoken exchanges, use the [Podcasts/interviews guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/746d8c8a-0c8a-4ba0-9f37-0e38ffdcf686) to follow how speakers develop and qualify ideas.

### 3. Select

- Choose patterns and details that directly support your interpretation.
- Prefer brief, precise evidence over long quotations or inventories of techniques.
- Ask what each choice does, why it suits this audience and purpose, and how it contributes to the text as a whole.

### 4. Construct

- State a focused thesis that answers the guiding question and offers an interpretation.
- Organize paragraphs around ideas or effects. Do not organize the essay as a tour of devices.
- Move from evidence to choice, effect, and significance. A useful test is: **what does this detail help the creator make the audience think, feel, notice, or accept?**

### 5. Verify

- Check that every paragraph advances the thesis.
- Remove claims that the evidence cannot support.
- Proofread for precise vocabulary, integrated quotations, sentence control, and clear transitions.

### Need another way in?

If the initial method leaves you unsure where to begin, try [SOAPSTone](/courses/language-literature/resources/eab78d37-cc35-476e-a70b-d1b674c8f512): Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, and Tone. It gives you prompts for an initial rhetorical reading; use the resulting observations to build your argument.

For poetry in Literature, [TPCASTT](/courses/literature/resources/81a5570b-6369-4557-b98b-9d8fa1be2f52) offers a different scaffold. Choose the tool that suits the text. Neither framework is a required essay structure.

## Avoid

Use this as a quick diagnosis when a response is not working.

### Interpretation problems

- Retelling the content without interpreting its significance.
- Making broad claims about symbolism without considering context.
- Discussing only the “big picture” or only tiny details, rather than connecting the two.
- Selecting evidence that is interesting but unrelated to the guiding question.

### Analysis problems

- Naming a device and stopping there.
- Using effects that could apply to almost any text: “grabs attention,” “creates an image,” or “makes the reader want to read on.”
- Treating every feature separately instead of noticing patterns and combinations.
- Assuming the creator’s intention when the text itself does not support the claim.

### Organization problems

- Beginning without a defensible thesis or clear line of inquiry.
- Organizing paragraphs by device instead of by an interpretive idea.
- Starting body paragraphs with line references or quotations before establishing the point.
- Repeating the introduction in the conclusion instead of explaining the larger significance of the reading.

## Criteria

These practical explanations help you use the criteria while planning and revising. They do not replace the full rubric.

### A · Understanding and interpretation

**What is the text communicating?** Show that you understand both its literal meaning and its larger implications. Develop a convincing interpretation and support it with well-chosen references. A textual reference can be a quotation or another precise reference to the text.

**What A looks like in Language & Literature Paper 1:** Establish what the text communicates and develop a supported interpretation of its purpose and audience. For an advertisement, distinguish what it claims about the product from what its evidence actually establishes.

**Check your work:** Does each claim about meaning, audience, or purpose have support in this particular text?

### B · Analysis and evaluation

**How does the text communicate it?** Explain how textual features and authorial choices create meaning. Evaluation means showing how and why those choices work within this particular text. Precise terminology can help, but naming a technique never substitutes for developed analysis.

**What B looks for in Language & Literature Paper 1:** Move from identifying a choice to explaining how it works. In the CDC example, naming the headline and photograph is a start; explaining how “attached” connects a smoking habit with visible oxygen tubing develops the analysis.

**Check your work:** Have I explained how the choices work together and why that relationship matters to the text’s purpose?

### C · Focus and organization

Establish a clear line of argument, develop it logically, and keep every paragraph relevant to the guiding question. There is no single required structure. Context belongs only where it advances the interpretation rather than interrupting it.

**What C looks like in Language & Literature Paper 1:** Build paragraphs around ideas that develop your answer. For example, establish how an advertisement presents a problem, then explain how it offers a response. Words, images, and layout can contribute to both stages.

**Check your work:** Does the order develop my argument, or could I swap the paragraphs without changing anything?

### D · Language

Communicate the analysis clearly with precise, varied, and appropriately formal language. Aim for control rather than ornate jargon. Integrate evidence smoothly and leave time to correct errors that interrupt meaning.

**What D looks like in Language & Literature Paper 1:** Choose precise wording over elaborate vocabulary. Identify the relevant detail, explain its contribution, and qualify claims about audience response. Use terminology when it makes that explanation clearer.

**Check your work:** Have I said exactly what the text invites readers to think or do, without assuming that everyone responds identically?


## Practice

Use short, repeatable drills before attempting another full paper:

1. **Five-minute orientation:** identify audience, purpose, text type, context, and first impression.
2. **Guiding-question rewrite:** express the question as a direct analytical task in your own words.
3. **Pattern hunt:** find three connected choices and explain the larger effect they create together.
4. **Thesis test:** write a thesis, then underline the part that offers an interpretation rather than a topic.
5. **Paragraph audit:** label the evidence, analytical verb, effect, and larger significance in one paragraph.

[Open Passage Practice](/practice/passages) to work with an unseen text and receive focused feedback on literary analysis.

## Field tools

Use a compact check before revising:

- Is my interpretation supported by precise references?
- Have I explained how choices shape meaning?
- Does each paragraph advance the response to the question?
- Is my language clear and precise?

For additional prompts, open [SOAPSTone](/courses/language-literature/resources/eab78d37-cc35-476e-a70b-d1b674c8f512) or [From observation to analysis](/courses/language-literature/resources/bfa6c8ee-0901-4cc2-b3fb-2070394d9432).

## Models

Explore Becky’s CDC advertisement in the worked-example panel alongside this guidance (below it on smaller screens). Follow the five steps, then open the analytical paragraph to see how a verbal choice and a visual detail support a single interpretation. Try transferring the method to the Amanda or Brian advertisement using the comparison prompts.

items.title: Paper 2
items.summary: Build a comparative argument about two literary works studied in the course.
items.body:
## Briefing

Build a comparative argument about two literary works in response to the chosen question. This guidance applies to both Literature and Language & Literature. Your interpretation should answer the question through the relationship between the works, supported by precise knowledge of their choices.

## Method

[Unpack a Paper 2 question](/resources/unpacking-questions#paper-2), then [try a past-paper question](#practice) and develop a comparative thesis.


### Unpack the question
Identify the central concept and the analytical task. Rephrase it as something you can argue about. Keep its particular wording in view as you select the works and evidence.

### Establish a basis for comparison
Find a meaningful relationship: a shared concern handled differently, a similar technique with different effects, or different routes to a comparable outcome. Difference alone is not yet an argument.

### Plan around claims
Write a comparative thesis and two or three supporting claims. For each claim, collect a precise moment from each work and explain how the writers' choices support the comparison. Choose a structure that lets those connections develop clearly.

### Sustain the relationship
Bring each discussion back to the question and the other work. Explain why the similarity or difference matters; a connective such as “similarly” cannot do that thinking for you.

## Avoid

- Two separate essays joined by a brief comparison at the end.
- Retelling events instead of examining how the writers present them.
- A prepared theme essay that only loosely fits the question.
- General claims about historical context that do not illuminate a textual choice.
- Treating balance as an identical word count rather than substantial attention to both works.

## Criteria

These practical explanations help you use the criteria while planning and revising. They do not replace the full rubric. The supplied Paper 2 rubric separates analysis into B1 and B2.

### A · Knowledge, understanding and interpretation

**What A looks like in Paper 2:** Use accurate knowledge of both works to develop an interpretation that answers the specific question. A well-chosen moment is useful because of what it helps you argue, not just because you remember it in detail.

**Check your work:** Have I explained what these moments reveal about the question, rather than summarized the works?

### B1 · Analysis and evaluation

**What B1 looks for in Paper 2:** Explain how textual features and broader authorial choices shape meaning. For example, a contrast between two endings becomes analysis when you explain how each ending changes our understanding of an earlier conflict.

**Check your work:** Have I explained how each writer creates the meaning I am comparing?

### B2 · Comparative analysis

**What B2 looks for in Paper 2:** Develop the significance of a similarity or difference between the works. Saying that both contain conflict identifies a connection; explaining how they give that conflict different causes or consequences develops a comparison.

**Check your work:** What does reading these works together help me argue about the question?

### C · Focus and organization

**What C looks like in Paper 2:** Sustain a clear answer and give both works substantial attention. Arrange the ideas so that each stage develops the comparison. A three-part plan can work, but the paragraphs need a reason to appear in that order.

**Check your work:** Does my next paragraph extend, complicate, or challenge what I have already established?

### D · Language

**What D looks like in Paper 2:** Make the comparison precise through clear sentences and well-integrated references. Explain the relationship itself rather than relying on words such as “similarly” or “however” to make it clear.

**Check your work:** Can I state the significant similarity or difference clearly, without vague phrases such as “they are both different”?

## Practice

Use the question-to-thesis activity below to begin a response with two works you have read. Start with a question from 2023–2025 or choose an earlier bank for more practice. You can return to each question and export your planning.

## Field tools

Make a compact planning grid: **claim · evidence from work A · evidence from work B · choices · significance of the comparison**. Fill it in before choosing paragraph order.

Return to [From observation to analysis](/courses/language-literature/resources/bfa6c8ee-0901-4cc2-b3fb-2070394d9432) when evidence is doing more describing than explaining.

## Models

### A useful comparative claim
“Although both works present authority as dependent on public performance, one exposes its fragility through interruptions in dialogue while the other reveals it through a narrator's distance.”

This is a structural illustration, not a claim about specified works. It identifies a relationship and distinct authorial choices; it still needs precise evidence and adjustment to the question.

items.title: Individual Oral
items.summary: Explore how a global issue is presented through close analysis and connections to the wider works.
items.body:
## Briefing

Explore how a global issue is presented through close analysis and discussion of the wider works.

**Language & Literature:** a literary work and a non-literary body of work.

**Literature:** two literary works, one originally written in English and one studied in translation.

The preparation principles below apply to both. Keep the relevant course's text-selection requirements in view.

## Method

### Focus the issue
Formulate an issue precise enough to analyze and broad enough to matter beyond a single text. Test whether both selections offer substantial evidence of its presentation.

### Select the extracts
Choose passages with significant authorial choices. An extract should give you opportunities for close analysis and meaningful connections beyond its boundaries.

### Move between close and wide
For each selection, explain how particular details present the issue, then connect them to the wider work or body of work. Plan those connections explicitly.

### Rehearse an argument
Use concise prompts to sustain a clear line of thought. Practice transitions and balanced attention; listen for places where you describe content instead of analyzing choices.

## Avoid

- Delivering a speech about the issue with the texts used as illustrations.
- Analyzing techniques without returning to the issue.
- Staying inside the extracts and neglecting the wider works.
- Making broad claims about the wider work without specific references.
- Reading a script instead of developing a controlled oral explanation.

## Criteria

These practical explanations help you use the criteria while planning and revising. They do not replace the full rubric.

### A · Knowledge, understanding and interpretation
Support an interpretation of the texts in relation to the global issue with precise references.

**What A looks like in the Individual Oral:** Use precise knowledge of both extracts and their wider works or bodies of work to interpret the global issue. Explain what the selected details reveal about that issue rather than giving a general talk about the topic.

**Check your work:** Can I support my reading of the issue in both the extract and the wider work or body of work?

### B · Analysis and evaluation
Explain how the creators' choices present the issue, in both the extracts and the wider works.

**What B looks for in the Individual Oral:** Explain how authorial choices present the global issue. Move from a specific detail to the meaning it creates, then show how that reading connects to choices beyond the extract. Identifying the issue alone is not analysis.

**Check your work:** Have I explained how the issue is presented, rather than only where it appears?

### C · Focus and organization
Maintain a coherent line of thought and give substantial attention to both selections.

**What C looks like in the Individual Oral:** Keep the global issue in view as you move through the oral. Give both selections substantial attention and make the relationship between extract analysis and wider discussion clear. The IO does not require a comparative argument.

**Check your work:** Can a listener follow why I am moving to this next detail and how it advances my discussion of the issue?

### D · Language
Speak clearly and accurately with language suited to analytical discussion.

**What D looks like in the Individual Oral:** Use clear, accurate language that works when spoken. Shorter sentences and explicit connections help a listener follow complex analysis. Use terms you can explain and pronounce confidently.

**Check your work:** When I listen back, can I follow the reasoning without seeing my notes?


## Practice

Give a one-minute explanation that connects one choice to the global issue. Then add a specific connection to the wider work.

Record a rehearsal and identify one passage that merely describes content. Replace it with an explanation of how a choice shapes meaning.

## Field tools

Use a preparation grid with five columns: **detail · choice · effect · relation to the global issue · wider-work connection**.

Return to [From observation to analysis](/courses/language-literature/resources/bfa6c8ee-0901-4cc2-b3fb-2070394d9432) to check the analytical steps in each example.

## Models

### A connection to develop
“In the extract, [specific choice] presents the issue as […]. Elsewhere in the work, [precise moment] develops or complicates this through […].”

The second example should extend the interpretation. Merely stating that the issue occurs elsewhere does not explain how the writer presents it.

items.title: SOAPSTone: a rhetorical reading scaffold
items.summary: A second way into speeches, advertisements, and other rhetorical texts.
items.body:
## When to use it
If you are unsure where to begin with a persuasive text, use these six prompts to gather initial observations. Select the observations that help answer the guiding question; the acronym is a reading aid, not an essay structure.

## The six prompts
- **Speaker:** who speaks, and whose authority or experience does the text draw on? Distinguish a quoted voice from the organization publishing it.
- **Occasion:** what situation gives the text its purpose? Use supplied context and textual evidence; leave unknown details unknown.
- **Audience:** who is addressed? Identify clues in language, images, assumed knowledge, and the action requested.
- **Purpose:** what does the text invite that audience to think, feel, or do?
- **Subject:** what is it about at the literal level? Keep this distinct from its persuasive purpose.
- **Tone:** what attitude comes through, and where does it change? Support your description with particular choices.

## Turn notes into analysis
For the CDC Becky advertisement, distinguish the CDC as publisher from Becky as the personal voice. Then connect the warning tone of the headline with the encouraging offer of help. Explain why that movement might matter to a smoker considering quitting.

Choose two or three connected observations and develop an interpretation. Avoid writing six disconnected paragraphs simply to complete the acronym.

items.title: Infographic
items.summary: How infographics combine information, design and persuasion, with a worked public-health example.
items.body:
## What is an infographic?

An infographic communicates information through a deliberate combination of words, images and layout. It can make a complex idea easier to grasp, organize information for quick reference, or make an argument appear clear and compelling. Some contain charts and statistics; others explain a process or give instructions without plotting any data. Don't presume objectivity just because it seems more "data-driven." Look to see WHAT data is being chosen, and consider what's left out. The IB really loves infographics. 

Read it as a complete text. A number, icon or color acquires meaning through its relationship with the surrounding words and design (the context). 

## Uses and purposes

- **Explain:** turn a process, system or unfamiliar concept into labeled stages, diagrams or examples.
- **Inform:** summarize research, report a situation or give readers information they can retrieve quickly.
- **Compare:** align alternatives, changes over time or differences between groups.
- **Persuade:** select and arrange information to support a position, raise concern or encourage a decision.
- **Guide action:** translate advice into steps, targets, precautions or practical choices.

Purposes often overlap. A charity may use statistics to inform readers while encouraging donations; a public-health organization may explain a risk while promoting a behavior. Identify the particular combination rather than assuming that every infographic is neutral information.

## Common features and techniques

### Headline and framing claim

What is presented as the main finding or problem?

**Possible analysis:** The headline can give the details a preferred interpretation. Check whether the evidence supports its wording.

### Visual hierarchy and salience

What stands out through scale, contrast, position or white space?

**Possible analysis:** Prominence can prioritize a fact or instruction. Explain why that element matters to the message. Don't oversell it; a paragraph on how bold text makes something stand out, a lengthy explanation of the font selection, the size of the text--those are all valid things to observe, but they slip into description with obvious effects quickly.

### Layout and reading path

How do columns, panels, arrows or numbering connect ideas?

**Possible analysis:** Arrangement may suggest sequence, comparison or cause and effect. Those relationships still need scrutiny. Why are these elements arranged the way they are? Don't make your default "engage the reader"--that says almost nothing.

### Icons, pictograms and illustrations

What do images represent, simplify or leave out?

**Possible analysis:** Familiar images can make an abstract idea easier to recognize, but may also oversimplify a complex issue. 

### Labels and anchorage

How do words direct the interpretation of an image or number?

**Possible analysis:** A label can narrow an image's meanings; a qualification—a limit or condition—can change what a prominent figure means. Often, a guiding question will ask youy how the text and image work together, and this is one aspect of that. 

### Color and typography

How are elements grouped, distinguished or emphasized?

**Possible analysis:** Establish the practical relationship before claiming a symbolic effect. Color associations depend on context. Green might be "eco-friendly" in one infographic, but signal money in another. Be cautious about applying universal effects.

### Numbers and data displays

Are figures measurements, recommendations, comparisons or estimates?

**Possible analysis:** Numerical precision may lend authority. Check units, scales, denominators and qualifications where applicable. Precision can also be used to make something sound more "science-based" (like how 51.2 sounds more "thorough" than 51). 

### Sources and institutional identity

Who publishes the text, and whose evidence does it use?

**Possible analysis:** Logos and source lines may establish credibility, but do not independently prove a claim.

### Calls to action

What is the reader asked to do next?

**Possible analysis:** Imperatives, links or targets may turn understanding into a proposed action.

These are common possibilities, not requirements. Do not invent a chart, axis or legend where the text has none.

## Audience and appeal

Start with **who needs this information and who can act on it**. The people pictured or discussed are not necessarily the intended readers. Support your inference through vocabulary, assumed knowledge, publication context, examples, and the action requested. If it's an infographic that advocates building more bike lanes, ask yourself: who could do something with this information? The average person can't decide how to zone a city, so who can? 

Then ask what the audience is being offered:

- **Usefulness and accessibility:** brief labels, familiar examples and clear grouping can reduce the effort of finding or applying information.
- **Reason and evidence:** comparisons, quantities and explanations may make a claim appear well supported. Examine the reasoning as well as the appearance of precision.Precision can also be used to give a claim more "authenticity" than it deserves. 
- **Credibility:** named sources, professional language and institutional identity can invite trust. Consider whether the authority is relevant to this claim. 
- **Emotion and values:** depictions of risk, wellbeing, fairness or belonging may connect the information to concerns the audience recognizes.
- **Achievable action:** practical steps or a choice of actions can help readers see how they could follow the advice.

Turn the audience inference into analysis: **Which specific choice addresses which plausible concern, and how does that serve the purpose?** Do not assume all readers respond identically or invent demographic details without evidence.

## Different kinds of infographic

- **Statistical:** inspect quantities, units, denominators, time periods, scales and sources. Ask whether the headline overstates the data.
- **Process or timeline:** inspect sequence, stages, arrows, dates and gaps. Ask what is made to seem simple or inevitable.
- **Comparison:** inspect matched categories and visual alignment. Ask whether the comparison is like for like.
- **Instruction or explainer:** inspect labels, grouping, examples, thresholds and calls to action. Ask how information becomes usable.

A single text may combine several of these approaches. Choose what to examine according to what the infographic needs to explain or persuade readers to do.

## A practical reading method

1. Establish the subject, context and likely purpose before listing techniques.
2. Identify the audience using details from the text and any supplied context.
3. Trace the overall argument or suggested reading path.
4. Select two or three significant relationships between words, images, numbers and arrangement.
5. Explain how those choices shape meaning for that audience. Check qualifications, omissions and alternative readings.

A strong response explains the combination: what does the wording clarify about the picture, or the arrangement imply about the information? Avoid organizing an entire essay as an inventory of colors, fonts and devices.

## Vocabulary and further guidance

Useful starting terms include **salience, visual hierarchy, reading path, grouping, pictogram, anchorage, contrast, qualification, imperative** and **ethos**. Use a term only when it makes your explanation more precise.

- [Literary, rhetorical and image-analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference)
- [Analytical verbs, tone words and sentence stems](/resources/analytical-language)
- [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d)
- [Purdue OWL: analyzing visual documents](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/visual_rhetoric/analyzing_visual_documents/index.html)

## Worked example

## Start here

Apply the overview to one complete infographic. Follow the relationship between its words, images and arrangement, then test your own reading against specific details.

### The text

**Physical activity for early years (2019)** is a public-health infographic issued by the UK Department of Health and Social Care. It translates recommendations into benefits, daily targets and activities. The source panel preserves the 2019 design; the current government download has been revised.

**Practice guiding question:** How do words and visual choices make the advice feel both authoritative and achievable?

First, look at the whole infographic without reading the model. What stands out? What does it ask someone to do? Use the close-up buttons beside the source to check small details. An initial reading might be: *the infographic presents children's activity as worthwhile, measurable and possible through ordinary play.* Treat that as a claim to test.

Work through **Audience and purpose → Read the design → Build a response**. Use **Vocabulary in action** to name relevant choices, and return to the Overview when meeting another infographic. The final section gives you a place to write and export your own analysis.

## Audience and purpose

### 1. Separate the subject from the audience

The subject is young children's activity. That does not make young children the principal readers. Adults usually arrange the activities and interpret the daily targets. The small explanatory labels and references to age groups support a reading aimed at **parents, caregivers and early-years practitioners**.

The [government publication page](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/physical-activity-guidelines-early-years-under-5s) also identifies **health professionals** as users of the resource when explaining activity. That is supplied context. Our inference about caregivers comes from what the text asks readers to understand and do. Distinguish these two kinds of evidence.

### 2. Ask what this audience values or needs

The benefits include sleep, social skills, health and readiness for school. Those are plausible adult concerns. The mix allows different readers to find a reason to value activity: a parent may notice sleep; a practitioner may notice learning and coordination. These are possibilities supported by the wording, not facts about every reader.

Do not invent a precise age, income, gender or family situation for the audience without evidence. “Mothers aged 25–40” is less defensible than “adults responsible for young children's routines.”

### 3. Turn the inference into analysis

Naming an audience is only the beginning. Connect **a reader's likely concern → a specific choice → the purpose it serves**.

- **Observation:** the introduction promises that active children “sleep better.”
- **Audience inference:** caregivers may value benefits that affect everyday routines as well as long-term health.
- **Analytical move:** By including sleep among the benefits, the infographic makes activity relevant to daily care, giving adults a practical reason to adopt its recommendations.

### 4. State a purpose as an action or change

“Inform people about exercise” is broad. Here, the text seeks to **encourage adults to provide regular, age-appropriate movement by making the recommendation understandable and manageable**. Informing and persuading can work together: the numerical target clarifies the advice, while the benefits and activity choices make acting on it more attractive.

Useful sentence stem: **For readers who need to ___, the combination of ___ and ___ presents ___ as ___.** Fill it with evidence; remove the frame if it makes the sentence awkward.

## Read the design

### 1. Benefits make the target worth considering

The six small benefit panels combine familiar icons with brief labels. The heart's label narrows its meaning toward health and weight; the building blocks connect play with learning. This is **image–text anchorage**: words help direct the interpretation of an image.

The repeated panels create **grouping**, making several benefits easy to scan. Their effect depends on their content: they present activity as contributing to several aspects of a child's life, rather than only physical strength. That gives adult readers several possible motivations.

### 2. A number becomes a memorable instruction

The large orange clock and oversized **180** create **salience**: they stand out through scale and contrast. The clock's familiar shape connects the recommendation with daily time. This is an **iconic representation of time**, not a pie chart showing proportions.

Read the surrounding words as carefully as the number. **“At least”** qualifies the target as a minimum; **“per day”** establishes frequency; **“for children 1–5 years”** identifies the group. These details prevent the large figure from becoming a universal instruction for every child. The separate Under-1s panel makes the age distinction visible.

### 3. The activity tiles make the instruction feel possible

The teal tiles offer a range of named actions, including walking, dancing, messy play and playground activity. Their repeated format creates **visual consistency** and presents them as related possibilities. The short labels anchor the simplified **pictograms**.

Read these tiles beside **“Every movement counts.”** The inclusive “every” and the variety of everyday actions widen what can count as activity. The combination can make the substantial daily target seem achievable through familiar routines. The stepped arrangement may also suggest building activity gradually, reinforcing the idea that small movements contribute to a larger goal. Test that reading against the tiles and slogan. It does not establish a literal sequence of activities for successive ages: the tiles have no age labels or arrows specifying such an order.

### 4. The ending combines encouragement with authority

**“Get Strong. Move More. Break up inactivity”** uses three short **imperatives**. The parallel commands give the ending a brisk rhythm and leave the reader with actions to remember. The tone is directive but also encouraging, especially after the page has supplied examples of what to do.

The source line naming the UK Chief Medical Officers establishes **institutional authority**, or **ethos**. It gives readers a reason to regard the advice as medically informed. It does not, by itself, display the underlying studies or prove that every recommendation has been demonstrated on this page.

### Put the parts together

A possible reading path is **reasons → target → practical options → call to action**. The eye may instead go straight to the orange clock. Describe the hierarchy and relationships the design makes available, rather than claiming every reader follows one route.

## Build a response

### A possible thesis

The infographic combines a clear daily target with pictures of familiar activities to present exercise as an important but manageable part of caring for young children. Its medical source gives the advice authority, while the examples show adults how to act on it.

This answers the practice question with an interpretation. It gives the response something to demonstrate; it does not simply promise paragraphs about color, numbers and images.

### A plan organized around meaning

1. **Make activity matter:** connect the benefit labels and icons to adult concerns about care and development.
2. **Make the recommendation usable:** examine the prominent number, its qualifying language and the separate age groups.
3. **Make action feel achievable:** connect the activity tiles, the inclusive slogan and the closing commands.

Bring language and visual choices together within each idea. Select enough evidence to develop a reading; you do not need to mention every tile.

### Worked analytical paragraph

The infographic makes the daily target seem manageable by placing a large orange clock beside familiar activities. The oversized “180” emphasizes how much movement is recommended. The tiles for walking, dancing and messy play then show ordinary ways to reach that target. “Every movement counts” reinforces this reassurance. The word “every” suggests that small activities matter too, rather than limiting exercise to organized sport. For adults planning a child’s day, the number establishes a goal and the images offer ways to meet it. This combination encourages readers to take the recommendation seriously without making it seem out of reach.

### Why this develops analysis

- **Interpretation:** the opening proposes a relationship between a demanding target and manageable action.
- **Evidence:** the paragraph names visible features and quotes wording that actually appears.
- **Explanation:** it connects the tiles to the breadth of “every.” It goes beyond naming color or listing activities.
- **Audience and purpose:** it explains why that relationship could matter to adults organizing care.
- **Evaluation:** it judges the contribution of the combined choices to the larger purpose. It does not guarantee compliance or claim a mark for the paragraph.

This is one defensible reading. Another response could examine whether the very prominent number overshadows the smaller qualifications. Support that judgment with the relative size and placement of those details.

[Develop an introduction](/resources/paper-1-introductions?example=language-literature) or practice the movement [from observation to analysis](/resources/observation-to-analysis).

## Vocabulary in action

Use a term to make an observation more precise. Follow it with evidence and interpretation; the terminology is not the analysis.

### Attention and organization

- **Salience:** how much an element stands out. *The orange clock gives the daily target greater salience than the source line.*
- **Visual hierarchy:** the ordering of attention through size, position and contrast. *The large target stands out, while the smaller wording explains who it applies to.*
- **Reading path:** a route the design suggests through its elements. *The movement from benefits to activities links motivation with action.*
- **Grouping / proximity:** placing items together so they appear connected. *Repeated tiles group varied actions as possible forms of movement.*
- **Contrast:** a difference that distinguishes elements. *Orange separates the target and infant guidance from the teal activity tiles.*
- **Typography:** the treatment of lettering, including size and weight. *The bold numeral makes the recommendation conspicuous; its smaller surrounding words specify its scope.*

### Words, images and persuasion

- **Pictogram:** a simplified picture representing an object or action. *The walking pictogram makes an ordinary activity recognizable at a glance.*
- **Anchorage:** wording that directs how an image is understood. *The health-and-weight label narrows the heart icon's possible meanings.*
- **Imperative:** a grammatical command. *The closing imperatives turn the explanation into a prompt to act.*
- **Qualification:** wording that limits or specifies a claim. *“At least” defines a minimum rather than an exact or maximum duration.*
- **Register:** language suited to a situation and audience. *Everyday activity labels make the official advice easy to understand.*
- **Ethos:** an appeal to credibility or authority. *The named medical officers lend institutional credibility to the advice.*

### When there is a statistical chart

**Encoding** is how a visible feature represents information: bar length might represent a count. A **legend** explains a code, while an **axis**, **baseline** and **unit** establish how quantities should be read. **Proportion** describes a part in relation to a whole. Those terms are useful for actual data displays; the clock in our example does not plot a distribution.

### Verbs that do analytical work

Choose a verb that names the actual action: **emphasizes** draws attention to a detail; **groups** brings details together; **qualifies** limits a claim; **contrasts** highlights a difference. Terms such as **anchors** and **positions** can be useful, but explain what the caption helps readers see or what view the text invites them to take.

Try: **The [precise choice] emphasizes/qualifies/contrasts ___, inviting [supported audience] to understand ___ as ___.** Use a cautious verb when the effect cannot be guaranteed. See [analytical verbs and tone vocabulary](/resources/analytical-language) for a wider bank.

## Avoid and revise

### Naming instead of explaining

**Thin:** “The bright color grabs attention.”

**Developed:** “The orange target contrasts with the teal activity tiles, making the daily recommendation conspicuous while visually separating it from the menu of ways to meet it.”

### Guessing an audience

**Thin:** “It is for children because there are cartoons.”

**Developed:** “Although the pictograms depict play, the age-specific targets and references to school readiness address adults who plan young children's routines.”

### Turning a possibility into a certainty

**Thin:** “The pictures make every parent exercise with their child.”

**Developed:** “The familiar activities can make the recommendation appear feasible for caregivers, although the page cannot establish how readers will act.”

### Misreading what a number does

**Incorrect:** “The pie chart proves that children spend 180 minutes exercising.”

**Accurate:** “The clock-shaped callout presents a recommended minimum. It does not report observed behavior or divide a whole into proportions.”

### Treating color as a fixed code

Do not assume orange always means energy or teal always means health. Begin with how the colors distinguish, group or emphasize elements in this particular design. A symbolic interpretation needs additional support.

## Practice and transfer

### Before looking at the model again

Choose one relationship: **benefit icons and labels**, **the number and its qualifications**, or **the activity tiles and the slogan**. Explain how that relationship shapes the message for an audience you can support with evidence. Use the writing space below.

### Transfer the method

On your next infographic, record its purpose, the audience evidence and what it needs to explain or persuade readers to do before choosing terminology. Then ask which features actually matter. An infographic explaining a process may require a reading of sequence; a charity infographic may require scrutiny of statistics and a donation appeal. Reuse the questions, not a paragraph plan designed for a different text.

For a full response, return to [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d). For another explanation of visual analysis, see [Purdue OWL: analyzing visual documents](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/visual_rhetoric/analyzing_visual_documents/index.html).

## Additional worked example: Cycling

## Read the policy argument

ITDP’s *The Benefits of Shifting to Cycling* makes a case for changing urban transport. Its argument moves from the practicality of short bicycle journeys to projected environmental and financial benefits, then to six actions that could help bring the change about.

The supplied question asks how text and images convey the overarching message. Look for their contribution to that developing case rather than writing separate inventories of colors, icons and statistics. The main claim is that cycling can make a worthwhile contribution within a wider shift toward sustainable transport.

Read both pages before using the close-ups. The numerical comparisons describe scenarios looking toward 2050, with costs accumulated over 2015–2050. They are historical projections in this source, not a report of outcomes already achieved. The walkthrough analyses how those projections are presented; it does not independently verify their modelling.

This is a more demanding companion to the early-years activity example. Both use accessible graphics, but here students need to distinguish a contribution from a total, and an achievable-looking proposal from a guaranteed outcome. The analysis and model writing are original teaching material, not an official marked response.

## Make a larger shift begin with familiar journeys

The opening bicycle illustration immediately identifies the subject, while “The Benefits” frames the material as a positive case for change. Green unifies the heading, route and later benefit figures. In this context, it reinforces the environmental argument that the words and emissions section make explicit; color alone would not establish that argument.

The first claim is that there is “huge potential” for more bicycle trips. Distance and time give that possibility a practical shape: the source says at least 35% of trips are under 5km and around 50% are under 10km, paired with journeys of under 20 minutes by bicycle and under 30 minutes by e-bike respectively.

The simplified street map translates these figures into a recognizable journey between buildings. A home sits along a dotted route, with bicycle and e-bike symbols linking travel distances to modes of transport. Readers can picture movement through ordinary urban space rather than encountering percentages alone.

This presentation makes a large transport change begin with familiar short trips. It does not establish that every trip within those distances is suitable for every person: terrain, access, safety and individual circumstances are not explored here. The analysis should explain how the graphic makes feasibility persuasive without adding claims it does not demonstrate.

## Frame the proposal as achievable but conditional

A globe accompanies the baseline: approximately 7% of urban trips are taken by bicycle and e-bike. The next block proposes a shift to 23% by 2050. The arrow-like division between the green blocks gives the comparison a visual direction, carrying the reader from a present condition toward a possible future.

The wording “a modest” frames that proposed share as manageable. It is still more than three times the stated starting share, so “modest” is a persuasive judgment rather than a neutral description of an insignificant change. The argument invites readers to see meaningful change as within reach.

Read the smaller wording with the headline figure. Cycling and e-bikes are part of a comprehensive move toward mass transit, walking and biking, and away from cars. The conditional “If we shift” leads into “then…” and the benefits that follow. The infographic offers a chain of reasoning about a scenario, not a promise that buying a bicycle automatically produces the stated global results.

Notice the shift in scale: familiar journeys on a map become a global share on a globe. That movement helps connect choices about urban travel with much larger outcomes.

## Separate cycling’s contribution from the whole scenario

The emissions chart compares approximately 4300 megatonnes of CO₂ under Business as Usual with approximately 2200 under the High Shift Cycling Scenario. The contrasting bar heights make the scenario’s lower projected emissions immediately visible, while the gray and green distinguish the alternatives.

Beside it, “We could avoid” introduces a large green figure of approximately 300 megatonnes. That number is not the entire difference between the two bars. The smaller explanation identifies it as a 7% reduction over Business as Usual due to cycling, within a 47% total reduction in the comprehensive scenario.

The dashed section near the top of the lower bar and the connecting arrow help locate the highlighted contribution within the larger comparison. The factory and smoke icon give the otherwise abstract emissions a recognizable visual reference. Words and graphics therefore work at two levels: the bars establish the larger change, while the annotation draws attention to cycling’s part in it.

A strong reading accounts for both the prominent figure and its qualification. Saying “cycling alone cuts emissions from 4300 to 2200 megatonnes” would erase the wider transport changes stated in the text. Equally, calling the figures merely “logos” would leave their actual relationship unexplained.

## Add an economic reason for the change

The second page extends the case with “And save cities,” linking financial benefit to the environmental benefit already presented. The large “USD 25 TRILLION” gives the potential saving prominence, and the smaller line specifies that it is over the next 35 years and due to cycling.

Again, the bars show a wider comparison: approximately USD 450 trillion spent under Business as Usual and USD 320 trillion under the High Shift Cycling Scenario. The roughly USD 130 trillion difference is not the same as the USD 25 trillion attributed to cycling. The arrow and dashed segment direct attention to the highlighted part rather than asking us to equate it with the whole gap.

These are cumulative transport costs for 2015–2050, not an annual budget or a payment that each city receives. Keeping the time frame and scale clear is part of interpreting the infographic accurately.

The row of bicycle, home, vehicle and building icons reconnects the enormous monetary figure with everyday urban life. The financial case also broadens the appeal: a reader concerned with city spending is given a reason to consider a change already presented as environmentally beneficial.

## Turn benefits into policy actions

“Six Ways to Make the Change” shifts from what could be gained to what could be done. The repeated arrangement of a circular illustration, bold verb and short explanation makes the recommendations easy to scan and gives them a common purpose.

The verbs—“Build,” “Implement,” “Invest,” “Plan,” “Remove” and “Adopt”—present action directly. Their objects reveal the scale of responsibility: infrastructure, bike-share schemes, public transport, urban planning, motor-vehicle incentives and management policies. This supports an audience inference that includes policymakers and transport planners, not only people deciding how to commute.

The icons work with the wording rather than replacing it. The bicycle lane identifies infrastructure; the shared bicycle illustrates a service; the crossed-out car sits beside a proposal to remove motor-vehicle incentives, not to ban every car. Reading the image alone could overstate that recommendation.

The footer names ITDP, describes its work on transport systems and policy, and includes the UC Davis Institute of Transportation Studies identity. These signals connect the infographic to specialist organizations. They support an impression of expertise, though the extract itself does not show the underlying modelling or a full account of its assumptions.

The ending makes the benefits actionable: change requires coordinated policy and infrastructure, matching the earlier explanation that cycling belongs within a comprehensive transport shift.

## Build an analytical response

### A possible thesis

The infographic presents cycling as a practical way to make urban transport more sustainable. Familiar journey images help readers picture the change, while environmental and financial comparisons show its potential benefits. The final policy actions make clear that these gains depend on coordinated changes, not just individual cyclists.

A response could develop three connected ideas: the presentation of feasibility, the translation of projected benefits into visible comparisons, and the move from benefits to institutional action. Bring language and image together within those ideas rather than assigning separate paragraphs to statistics, color and layout.

### Model paragraph

The emissions chart makes the projected benefit easy to see, but also limits what can be claimed for cycling alone. The gray Business as Usual bar reaches approximately 4300 megatonnes of CO₂, compared with approximately 2200 for the green High Shift Cycling Scenario bar. This large visual difference emphasizes the potential reduction. Beside it, the green “~300” highlights the part attributed to cycling. An arrow and a dashed segment connect this figure to the chart. The smaller wording explains that cycling’s 7% reduction is part of a 47% total reduction in the wider scenario. These details matter because the chart promotes cycling as one contribution to a broader change. It does not show that cycling alone would produce the whole reduction.

The paragraph explains a relationship between figures and design. It treats the qualification as part of the meaning rather than inconvenient fine print, and it analyses a projected benefit without reporting it as an established result.

## Practice and transfer

Write a paragraph connecting the cost comparison with one of the six policy actions. Explain how the infographic moves from an incentive to a proposed response, using a precise verbal detail and a precise visual detail.

Check three distinctions before exporting: cycling’s USD 25 trillion contribution versus the larger gap between scenarios; cumulative costs versus annual spending; and projected benefits versus observed outcomes.

For another infographic, ask what the most prominent number represents, what comparison surrounds it and what smaller wording qualifies it. Then explain how the design makes that particular argument accessible or persuasive. Do not assume that a large number is either self-explanatory or misleading simply because it is prominent.
