items.summary: Read how drawing, wording and panel arrangement work together, then examine Andy Singer’s ironic history of technology.
items.body:
## Reading a cartoon

A cartoon makes meaning through a deliberately drawn view of the world. It may entertain, criticize a public issue, expose a contradiction or invite recognition of an everyday frustration. Some make readers laugh; others unsettle or accuse. Begin with the particular situation and viewpoint rather than assuming that every cartoon is simply humorous.

Cartoons can appear as a single image, a short sequence of panels, an editorial cartoon, a comic strip or a webcomic. These categories overlap. A strip can make a political argument, while a single-panel cartoon can tell a small story through an implied before and after. Bear in mind that because the IB is global, you are highly unlikely to EVER see direct criticism of an individual, country, or specific company. The topics typically include things we can all agree on to some level: that AI is going to change the job market, that climate is a serious issue, literacy is good, etc. 

Your task is to explain how the drawing, wording and arrangement work together. A paragraph describing the picture followed by an unrelated paragraph on language usually misses the relationship that gives the cartoon its point.

## Situation, audience and target

Establish what is literally shown before explaining what it represents. Who or what is present? Where are they? What are they saying or doing? Labels, captions and recognizable objects may identify a public figure, institution or issue. If the context is not supplied, distinguish what you can infer from what you would need to research.

Identify the **target** of the humor or criticism. It might be a politician, an institution, a social habit, a belief about progress or the viewer’s own assumptions. The person drawn is not necessarily the person being attacked: a frustrated character may expose the failure of a system rather than become the object of ridicule.

Infer audience from the publication context, assumed knowledge, language and references. “Everyone” is rarely a useful audience description. Equally, do not invent a precise age or political position without evidence. Consider what the viewer must recognize for the joke or argument to work.

A cartoon expresses a viewpoint. Analyze how it makes that viewpoint persuasive or memorable without treating its simplified account as a neutral statement of fact.

## Text and image together

Different kinds of wording do different jobs. A **speech balloon** gives a character a voice; a **thought balloon** conventionally presents unspoken thought. A **caption** can establish a situation, comment on the image or supply a punchline. A **label** may tell us that an otherwise ordinary object represents an abstract idea or institution. A title can frame how the entire drawing is read.

Words may clarify the image, contradict it, or depend on it to complete a joke. A character’s claim to be in control means something different beside a visibly collapsing machine. The contradiction between statement and scene is the evidence; “text and image engage the audience” is too general.

Try a temporary removal test: what becomes unclear if you cover the wording, and what disappears if you read the wording without the drawing? Use the answer to explain the contribution of each mode and the meaning created by their combination.

Lettering also matters. Size, capitals, underlining, punctuation and placement can suggest emphasis or differentiate voices. Handwritten capitals may be a convention throughout the cartoon, so do not automatically read every capitalised word as shouting.

## Panels, sequence and visual arrangement

A **panel** is a framed unit of the cartoon. In a sequence, examine the reading order and what changes between panels. A **gutter**, the space between panels, can leave readers to infer elapsed time, movement or a connection between scenes. Two adjacent panels might compare situations rather than show consecutive moments in one person’s life.

Repetition makes differences visible. A repeated pose or viewpoint can hold one element steady while the setting, words or circumstances change. Ask what the comparison encourages us to conclude.

Within a panel, consider foreground and background, relative size, contrast and the distribution of detail. A crowded scene may suggest abundance, pressure or disorder; an isolated figure may suggest vulnerability, importance or distance. Choose the meaning supported by the actual relationships in the drawing.

Notice how the eye is led toward a caption, expression or final panel. A punchline may depend on a delay or reversal. A cartoon can also present its contrast all at once, leaving the viewer to compare rather than discover a hidden ending.

## Figures, objects and visual shorthand

Posture, gesture, facial expression, clothing and the distance between figures can establish relationships quickly. Describe a visible detail before naming the emotion or attitude it suggests. “The shoulders slump and the mouth turns down” supports a reading more clearly than “the figure looks negative.”

**Caricature** exaggerates recognizable features of a person or type. **Exaggeration** can also affect scale, numbers or a situation: a mountain of paperwork might make bureaucracy seem overwhelming. Explain what is enlarged and why that matters.

A **visual metaphor** presents one thing through another—for example, a policy drawn as a leaking boat. **Symbolism** gives an object significance beyond its literal role. Context and labels may establish the connection; do not assume every object is a symbol with a fixed meaning.

Cartoons often use stereotypes as shorthand. Identify what the shorthand asks viewers to recognize and how it supports the argument. You can also consider what it simplifies or excludes. Recognizing a stereotype does not require accepting it as an accurate account of a group or historical period.

## Humor, irony and the argument

**Incongruity** brings together things that do not fit an expectation. **Irony** can emerge from a gap between a claim and the situation, or between an expected outcome and the one shown. **Satire** uses humor, ridicule or exaggeration to expose a perceived fault. A cartoon can combine these, but naming all three is less useful than explaining the exact contradiction.

Ask why the joke matters beyond being funny. Does it make a familiar habit seem absurd, puncture a confident claim, invite self-recognition or make a powerful figure look vulnerable? The answer helps connect technique to purpose.

Keep the argument proportionate. A cartoon may challenge the assumption that a new invention solves every problem without claiming that all inventions are harmful. Its simplification is part of how it communicates, and can also be a limitation worth recognizing.

Use the [analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference) for visual and rhetorical terms, and [analytical language](/resources/analytical-language) to make effects precise. Avoid applying ethos, pathos and logos as an automatic three-paragraph plan. If emotion matters, name the emotion and explain what creates it.

## A method for Paper 1

1. Describe the situation briefly and accurately. Separate visible details from inferred context.
2. Identify the central contrast, contradiction or surprising connection. Follow any sequence of panels.
3. Connect precise words with precise visual details. Include framing, expression, arrangement or objects where they help explain the relationship.
4. State the viewpoint or criticism in a sentence that goes beyond the topic. “Technology” is a topic; a claim about what technology can or cannot change is an interpretation.
5. Build paragraphs around ideas and test the reading against a complicating detail. Does the cartoon criticize a product, a promise made about it, or the way people use it?

For the wider planning and writing process, return to [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d).

## Worked example

## Read the two panels together

Andy Singer’s *The History of Technology*, from the cartoon collection *No Exit*, places two seated figures side by side. The left figure wears an animal-skin garment in a natural landscape and says “ME NOT HAPPY.” The right wears a suit amid manufactured objects and says “STILL NOT HAPPY!”

The supplied question asks how text and image work together to communicate the cartoon’s message. Begin with the relationship: much has changed around the figures, yet their dissatisfaction persists. The cartoon challenges an easy equation between technological development and greater happiness.

Read the complete cartoon before examining details. Both panels remain together beside the commentary so that comparisons stay visible; select **Enlarge cartoon** for a closer view. This walkthrough and its model writing are original teaching material, not an official marked response.

## A grand title and a very small history

“The History of Technology” promises an account of a vast development. The image compresses it into just two scenes: a conventional prehistoric figure and a modern suited man. The gap between the panels asks the reader to supply the enormous passage of time and change that is not shown.

This is visual shorthand, not a factual timeline. The animal-skin clothing, natural surroundings and simplified “ME NOT HAPPY” establish the first figure as a familiar cartoon version of a prehistoric person. The suit, aircraft and manufactured objects establish the second as modern. We do not need to identify specific dates or cultures to follow the contrast.

The title makes the contrast about technological history; the speech balloons judge that history through personal happiness. The humor comes partly from reducing an expansive story of development to a blunt complaint that survives it.

*No Exit* is the collection’s name, as the supplied introduction explains. Its wording may resonate with the repeated dissatisfaction, but the argument should rest on the specific title, panels and dialogue rather than treating the collection label as a newly written caption.

## A changed setting, a repeated figure

The figures occupy comparable positions in the two tall panels. Both sit facing outwards, with similar lowered arms, narrowed eyes and open mouths. Their clothing changes, but the repeated posture and expression make them visual counterparts.

That continuity is crucial. The modern figure does not appear transformed by the objects around him. His appearance carries the earlier dissatisfaction across the panel boundary before “STILL” makes the connection explicit.

The figures can represent people in different eras without being the same individual. Calling this a literal before-and-after portrait of one man would overlook the title’s historical scale and the visual shorthand of the settings.

Avoid claiming that the first figure is happy because he is surrounded by nature. His own words deny it. The cartoon does not offer a simple story in which a contented past has been ruined by a miserable present: the repeated unhappiness is the point.

## From natural life to manufactured clutter

The left panel contains trees, flowers, birds, a sun and fish in water. The right replaces that environment with buildings, smokestacks, an aircraft and a dense accumulation of manufactured objects. Screens, appliances, a racket and a broken umbrella are piled around and beneath the suited figure. Some objects appear damaged, including the cracked screen.

Both panels contain plentiful detail. The useful contrast is therefore not merely “empty nature versus a busy city,” but the kinds of things that fill each scene. Natural life in the first gives way to manufactured objects and signs of industrial activity in the second.

The pile makes technological abundance look cumbersome and disorderly rather than comfortably organized around human needs. Smoke and damaged objects also allow a reading of environmental cost and waste. Keep that reading attached to what is visible; the cartoon does not provide a complete account of pollution or prove that every object is useless.

Most importantly, abundance surrounds a figure who remains dissatisfied. Read the objects with the expression and speech balloon: together, they undermine the expectation that having more technology necessarily means living more happily.

## Still not happy

“ME NOT HAPPY” establishes dissatisfaction in the left panel through a short, stereotypically simplified utterance. “STILL NOT HAPPY!” repeats “NOT HAPPY” but adds the word that connects the two scenes across time.

**“Still”** means the condition continues despite what has happened in between. The drawing supplies that intervening change: different clothing, an industrial skyline and a heap of manufactured goods. Without the image, we would not know what the complaint has survived; without “still,” the historical comparison would be less explicit.

The final exclamation mark adds force to the modern complaint. It can suggest frustration that so much development has failed to change this outcome. The capitals are used throughout the cartoon’s lettering, so they are weaker evidence of a special increase in volume than the added punctuation and the contrast itself.

The result is a pointed mismatch between material change and emotional continuity. This supports a criticism of technology’s promise of happiness, rather than a claim that no technology has ever brought any benefit.

## Build an analytical response

### A possible thesis

Singer contrasts two very different environments with figures who look equally unhappy to question whether technological progress makes life better. The repeated complaint, especially “still,” suggests that new possessions have not resolved an old dissatisfaction.

A response could first examine how title and panel arrangement compress historical change, then show how the repeated figure and altered complaint challenge its expected benefit. The objects, expressions and wording should work together within those ideas, rather than becoming separate lists of visual and verbal techniques.

### Model paragraph

The modern figure’s complaint challenges the idea that technological progress necessarily brings happiness. In the left panel, a figure in an animal-skin garment says “ME NOT HAPPY.” In the right, a man in a suit says “STILL NOT HAPPY!” Their similar positions, narrowed eyes and open mouths suggest that their feelings have barely changed. “Still” emphasizes this lack of change despite the aircraft, industrial buildings and manufactured objects around the modern man. These objects show how much his surroundings have developed, while his words suggest how little this has improved his satisfaction. The contrast questions the assumption that having more technology means living better.

The paragraph explains how specific words direct our reading of specific images. Its claim is qualified by “the assumption”: it analyses the cartoon’s challenge without converting a satirical comparison into proof that technology has no value.

## Practice and transfer

Write a paragraph connecting the title with the two environments. Choose at least one detail from each panel and explain how the repeated complaint changes our judgment of the contrast.

Before exporting, test your reading against the first figure’s unhappiness. Does your paragraph accidentally describe a happy past? Does it claim technology caused dissatisfaction when the first panel shows it already present?

For another cartoon, ask what changes, what stays the same, and which words make the relationship clear. If it has only one panel, look for a contrast within the scene or between a statement and the image. Follow the new cartoon’s particular argument rather than importing this one.

items.title: Blog post
items.summary: Read voice, structure and digital features in personal, travel, advice and opinion blogs, with an illustrated Oliver Emberton worked example.
items.body:
## What makes a blog post

A blog post is an individual entry on a website or blogging platform. It may tell a personal story, offer advice, explain an idea, review an experience or argue a position. A recognizable writer or organization usually gives the post a particular voice. Readers may encounter it through a search, a shared link or an ongoing relationship with the blog.

“Blog” tells us something about publication, but not everything about purpose. An opinion piece can appear on a blog; a business can publish helpful advice that also promotes its services. Begin by asking what this particular post offers its readers and what response it seeks.

Not every online article is a blog post, and not every blog is an informal diary. Use the supplied context and visible features to establish the form. A print extract may omit links, comments or other parts of the original page: analyze what is available rather than inventing a surrounding website.

## Audience, purpose and the writer’s role

A useful audience description identifies a shared interest, need or experience. “People interested in travel” is a start; “independent travellers looking for candid accounts of difficult journeys” explains more about why a writer might mix useful detail with self-deprecating humor. Do not assume that every blog targets teenagers or everyone who uses the internet.

Consider the role the writer adopts. Are they an experienced guide, a fellow beginner, a witty companion, a specialist or a campaigner? A writer may shift between roles: admitting a mistake can create common ground before offering advice. First-person language alone does not make a voice trustworthy. Explain what the writer shares, how they present it and why it matters to this audience.

Purposes can overlap. A post might entertain while challenging an assumption, or explain a problem before inviting a purchase or subscription. Distinguish the immediate purpose of the entry from the wider aims of its website. A newsletter link suggests an ongoing relationship; it does not prove that every paragraph is trying to sell something.

## Different kinds of blog post

- **Personal or reflective:** a selected experience and the writer’s response to it. How does a private experience become meaningful to other people?
- **Travel or lifestyle:** an account of places, routines or choices. How do description and the writer’s persona shape the experience being offered?
- **Advice or how-to:** a problem, explanation and proposed action. How does the writer earn the right to advise, and make the advice seem achievable?
- **Opinion or commentary:** a position on an issue or debate. How does the argument develop, and how are alternative views treated?
- **Specialist or organizational:** knowledge, updates or guidance for an interested community. How are expertise and accessibility balanced, and whose interests are served?

These overlap. A travel narrative can recommend a destination; a personal story can support an argument. Follow the post’s main movement rather than forcing it into a single box.

## Voice and the relationship with the reader

Look at how the writer makes contact. Direct address can invite, advise, flatter or challenge. Inclusive “we” may establish shared experience, but it can also make an assumption sound universal. Questions may invite reflection or steer readers toward an answer the writer immediately supplies.

Conversational language is a choice with a purpose. Contractions, asides, fragments and short paragraphs can create the pace of an informal exchange. Humor may make an awkward admission easier to share or make an opponent seem ridiculous. Identify the particular attitude: amused, impatient, reassuring, admiring or skeptical is more useful than simply “informal.”

Personal experience can help establish credibility, but experience in one situation does not automatically support a universal claim. Read anecdotes, qualifications, references and confident assertions together. Ask how the post makes its account seem worth trusting.

## Structure, images and digital features

Read the title as a promise: a useful answer, an unusual experience, a provocative claim or a reason to reconsider something familiar. Then follow how the post fulfills or complicates that promise. It might move through a journey, from anecdote to reflection, or from problem to explanation to advice. These are possibilities, not a compulsory blog structure.

Subheadings can organize an argument as well as help readers scan. A numbered list can make a difficult change seem finite and manageable. A short final sentence may turn reflection into a challenge or return to the opening with a changed meaning. Explain what the sequence achieves, rather than just reporting that there is a beginning, middle and end.

Images may supply evidence, establish atmosphere, illustrate an analogy or contradict the words. Connect a specific visual detail with nearby language. A diagram can simplify a claim and make it look authoritative; its appearance does not guarantee that it presents measured data.

When visible, dates, author profiles, links, comments and sharing tools help establish publication context and a relationship with readers. A link might support a claim or direct attention elsewhere. A comment section may enable responses, but its mere presence does not prove that readers agree. Do not spend a paragraph naming navigation buttons unless their arrangement contributes to your interpretation.

## Useful vocabulary and common traps

Use terminology when it sharpens the explanation:

- **Persona:** the version of themselves a writer presents to the reader. It is not necessarily a complete picture of the person.
- **Register:** language chosen for a particular situation and relationship, including degrees of formality.
- **Direct address:** speaking to the reader, often through “you.” Identify what the reader is being invited or pressured to do.
- **Anecdote:** a short account of an event. Explain how it supports the post’s wider purpose.
- **Extended metaphor:** a comparison developed across several details or stages of a text.
- **Imperative:** a command or instruction. Its effect depends on the voice and relationship already established.
- **Hyperlink:** a clickable connection to another location. Analyze its destination and wording when these are available.

Avoid a list of generic effects: “engages the reader,” “makes it relatable” and “adds credibility” need a specific explanation. What experience is recognized? Which claim seems more credible, and why?

Appeal labels are optional. If discussing emotion, name it and show how it is developed. Credibility can be built through the post’s voice and evidence as well as borrowed from reputation. Reasoning means the connection between a claim and its support, not simply the presence of a number.

For further terms and examples, use the [analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference) and [analytical language bank](/resources/analytical-language).

## A practical reading method

1. Establish the writer, publication context, likely audience and main purpose from the supplied evidence.
2. State the title’s promise. What does the reader expect to gain?
3. Trace the post’s movement. Note changes in focus, tone or the writer’s role.
4. Choose connected details: for example, an anecdote and its later lesson, or an illustration and the claim it makes easier to accept.
5. Form an interpretation about how the post shapes the reader’s understanding or response. Organize paragraphs around that interpretation, not a checklist of blog features.
6. Test the reading against a qualification or complication. Does the ending soften an earlier claim? Does a joke make the voice less authoritative or more approachable?

For planning and writing a complete response, return to [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d).

## Worked example

## Read the whole post

Oliver Emberton’s “If you want to follow your dreams, you have to say no to all the alternatives” offers advice to readers who want to achieve ambitious goals but feel pulled in too many directions. Its central claim is that progress requires choosing what to pursue and what to postpone or refuse.

The supplied question asks: **How do authorial choices help to create a persuasive message?** A useful starting interpretation is that Emberton makes focus feel both understandable and necessary: he turns competing desires into a playful visual problem, gives his solution an air of certainty, then offers actions readers can take.

Read both pages before the close-ups. Page 1 establishes the problem and the benefits of concentration; page 2 turns that account into five instructions and returns to the title’s demand. The visible newsletter and “Best of” links place the entry within an ongoing personal blog, but the main argument is carried by the post itself.

This is the exam version cataloged as May 2024, TZ1, Text 1. The current online post contains additional words and images; they are not evidence for this reading. The commentary, thesis and model paragraph here are original teaching material, not an official marked response.

## Make divided attention recognizable

The title joins an attractive ambition, “follow your dreams,” to an unwelcome condition: “you have to say no.” It promises help while challenging the assumption that pursuing more opportunities always brings us closer to success. The second-person “you” makes that choice the reader’s own.

The opening makes the problem less forbidding. “Our brains behave like a beachball filled with bees” gives competing impulses a comic physical form. In the first illustration, bees inside a ball want a book, a new job and a kitten. These mismatched desires give visible shape to the pull of several goals at once. The surrounding prose adds exercise, Spanish and pizza, moving between self-improvement and immediate pleasure.

The inclusive “our” and repeated “we” present this divided attention as a shared experience. Emberton initially speaks as someone who recognizes the difficulty, rather than scolding the reader from outside it. The short “Let’s fix that” then changes his role: a companion in the problem becomes a guide toward the solution.

Connect the image to that shift. The playful comparison makes the problem easy to recognize; the confident invitation suggests it can be controlled. “Humor engages the reader” would miss what the humor helps the writer explain.

## Make even good ideas compete

“The curse of the ‘great idea’” challenges a comforting explanation for failure: perhaps we only need a better idea. The imagined reader has already thought of Google, Amazon and Facebook, yet would get “absolutely nowhere” by attempting all three simultaneously. Recognizable examples of business success make the imagined loss striking.

The second illustration carries the earlier comparison forward. Three bees aim toward three different companies. Individually attractive ambitions become competing directions, so the problem appears to be their combination rather than their quality. The progression from a kitten to global companies extends the claim from everyday distraction to exceptional ambition.

The instruction to “Imagine” gives the reader a role in this scenario, while the absolute conclusion leaves little space for an alternative outcome. It is a thought experiment, not a documented case study. Its persuasive force comes from making the writer’s account easy to picture and hard to dismiss, rather than from proving that every person with several goals will fail.

## Give focus the appearance of certainty

The next section raises the stakes. Asking what the reader would do if their own life and the lives of loved ones depended on success introduces fear of loss into an otherwise playful explanation. Emberton immediately supplies the answer: “You’d simply drop everything else.” The hypothetical danger makes focus seem an obvious necessity.

The graph gives this claim a different kind of authority. Its descending curve sets “ACHIEVEMENT” against “NUMBER OF DIRECTIONS,” with a large bee near the high end and smaller bees near the low end. Above it, the equation presents achievement as potential divided by directions squared. The metaphor now resembles a measurable relationship: more directions seem to reduce achievement by a precise rule.

That precision should be analyzed carefully. The graph has no numerical scale or cited measurements, and the post does not establish its equation through research. It visually reinforces Emberton’s reasoning about divided effort; it does not demonstrate a scientific law of success. The later claim that an extra direction will “quarter” achievement extends this impression of certainty. The formula and prose should not be reported as verified facts.

The references to “Edison to Einstein” also associate focus with admired achievement. Those names give the claim weight, but the post does not examine their lives in detail. A strong response explains how the combination of famous examples, mathematical form and confident language makes the advice seem authoritative.

## Turn the explanation into action

“How to tame the swarm” returns to the bees while promising control. The numbered list breaks a large demand into five named actions: “Aim higher,” “Limit to three,” “Put it off,” “Beware your idle wants” and “Line up your bumblebees.” Bold imperatives make the advice easy to scan and present the writer as someone with a usable method.

The instructions vary in attitude. “Put it off” makes selection less final: an ambition can wait rather than disappear. “Beware,” by contrast, makes apparently harmless desires threatening. “They are deadly” sharply exaggerates the cost of distraction, reinforcing the risk of ignoring the advice. Read that warning alongside the hopeful promise of achieving more.

The list also qualifies the title’s apparent demand to reject every alternative. The reader may keep separate goals for work, home and the weekend, while the fifth point permits goals that support one another. A healthier person might be a better leader; in the established comparison, the bees now push in the same direction.

This adjustment matters to persuasion. The advice remains firm, but becomes easier to imagine living with. The reader is being asked to organize effort around compatible priorities, not simply to abandon every interest except one.

## Return to the price of ambition

The ending gathers the bees, exceptional achievers and rejected opportunities into one account of success. Its repeated return to “said no” makes refusal sound like an active choice that creates progress, rather than a loss of possibility.

The final paragraph echoes the title but adds “the power” to follow dreams. Selection has become a source of agency. “It’s not easy” briefly acknowledges the difficulty, while “if that’s for you” leaves the reader an apparent choice. The final “price” presents sacrifice as the cost attached to an attractive outcome.

That movement gives the post coherence: a shared feeling of being pulled around becomes a promise of control, followed by instructions and a challenge. The colorful bees keep the explanation approachable while the repeated certainties make its recommendation forceful. A reading should account for both qualities rather than describing the entire tone as simply friendly.

## Build an analytical response

### A possible thesis

Emberton uses the comparison with bees to help readers recognize how competing ambitions divide their attention. His illustrations make the problem easy to picture, while direct instructions present focused effort as a way to make progress.

### Choose a manageable argument

A response could develop three connected ideas: first, how the post establishes a shared problem; next, how it makes focus seem necessary and authoritative; finally, how it turns that claim into usable advice. This is one possible organization, not a required three-part formula. Select the strongest evidence for your interpretation; a timed response need not cover every detail in this walkthrough.

### Model paragraph

Emberton makes divided attention easy to understand by giving it a playful visual form. He compares the brain to a “beachball filled with bees,” suggesting desires pushing in different directions. The illustration develops this idea through wishes for a book, a new job and a kitten. These examples show how major ambitions can compete with smaller wants. By using “our” and “we,” Emberton includes himself in the problem instead of simply blaming the reader. “Let’s fix that” then shifts from recognizing the difficulty to promising action. Its confidence prepares readers for his advice about choosing a direction. The image therefore helps explain why progress can stall and why focus might help.

The paragraph follows one idea through comparison, illustration and voice. It uses a few short quotations and explains their relationship. It does not need a separate sentence naming each appeal, or a claim that every reader must be persuaded.

## Practice and transfer

Write a paragraph explaining how the final advice makes focus seem achievable. Connect one bold instruction with its explanation, then consider how the fifth point qualifies the title. Aim to show how the advice develops the earlier comparison rather than just listing commands.

Alternatively, explain how the graph makes the claim look authoritative. Distinguish the reasoning being illustrated from evidence that would establish the mathematical relationship. Analyze the effect of the presentation without turning your response into a fact-checking essay.

For another blog post, begin again with its purpose and movement. A travel writer may build a relationship through an unfolding experience rather than giving instructions; a reflective writer may end with uncertainty. Transfer the questions about voice, structure and reader response, not Emberton’s particular formula for success.

items.summary: Trace a position through reasoning, tone and the relationship with readers, with a worked example from The Beast’s netball column.
items.body:
## What opinion and commentary do

Opinion writing puts forward a judgment and gives readers reasons to consider it. It may recommend action, challenge a familiar assumption, defend a value or offer a new way of understanding an issue. Commentary often interprets an event or trend through a particular perspective. The two overlap: both ask us to consider how a writer turns information into a position.

A piece need not sound solemn to make an argument. A humorous sports column can recommend what a community should value; a reflective personal essay can challenge a public attitude. Begin with the position the text develops, not the seriousness of its topic or tone.

Publication alone does not determine genre. A newspaper or a website such as The Conversation can publish different kinds of writing. A news report primarily reports events; an explainer primarily helps readers understand a subject; an opinion piece advances a judgment. These purposes can overlap. Use the supplied context, wording and structure to identify what the particular text is doing.

## Forms, audience and publication context

- **Signed opinion article or op-ed:** an identifiable writer advances a position, often about a public issue. Their argument need not represent the publisher’s view.
- **Editorial:** a piece usually presented as the publication’s institutional position, rather than one contributor’s personal view. Check how authorship is identified.
- **Column:** writing associated with a recurring voice, topic or slot. Its appeal may depend as much on the writer’s manner as on the position taken. Do not invent a publication schedule from one extract.
- **Personal commentary:** an experience becomes a way into a larger issue. Ask how the writer moves from an individual case to a broader judgment.
- **Satirical commentary:** humor, irony or exaggeration exposes something the writer finds foolish or objectionable. Not every funny opinion piece is a sustained satire.

Describe the audience through interests, values or assumptions supported by the text. A sports column might address readers who enjoy rivalry and recognize local teams; a policy article may explain technical terms for readers outside government. “The general public” rarely explains enough on its own.

Headlines, bylines, publication labels, images and captions can establish a subject and an expected voice before the argument begins. Discuss these when they help explain the reading. A logo is not automatically proof that a claim is reliable.

## Find the claim and follow the reasoning

Distinguish the **topic** from the **position**. “Public transport” names a topic; “the city should make buses free because access matters more than fare revenue” states a position and a reason. An opinion piece may announce its position immediately or reveal it gradually through anecdote, questions or contrast.

Track the connection between a claim and its support. Evidence might include examples, observations, quotations, research or personal experience. Ask what it actually establishes. A striking individual story may illustrate a problem without proving how widespread it is. A statistic only helps an argument when its population, comparison and relevance are clear.

Notice assumptions: values or beliefs the reader is expected to share. A claim about what a nation should celebrate might rely on fairness, achievement, popularity or belonging. A writer can persuade partly by changing which of those standards seems most important.

Look for alternative views. A **concession** accepts part of another position; a **rebuttal** challenges it. Neither is a compulsory paragraph. Explain what acknowledging a difficulty does here: it might make the position more measured, anticipate resistance or prepare a shift in the grounds of the argument.

## Tone, voice and credibility

Tone is the attitude conveyed by the writing toward its subject, readers or other people. Name that attitude precisely and support it with language. “Critical” is a start; “impatient with official excuses” identifies both the attitude and its target. Tone can change within a paragraph or combine qualities, such as affectionate teasing.

Read diction, punctuation, sentence shape and imagery together. A short interruption may overturn a serious-sounding claim. A parenthetical aside may invite the reader into a shared joke. Repeated inclusive pronouns may suggest agreement before the writer has established that everyone agrees.

Distinguish writer, persona and quoted voices. A columnist may present themselves as an ordinary, fallible observer to build rapport. Quoted insults may be the attitudes being mocked rather than the writer’s own position. Read what happens before and after a phrase before deciding whose view it expresses.

Credibility can come from expertise, but also from candour, fair treatment of objections or precise evidence. Humor may help a writer seem approachable while weakening their appearance of seriousness. Those effects can coexist. Explain the trade-off instead of deciding that every choice simply “makes the writer credible.”

## Structure and the reader’s changing response

Map what each part of the text does. An opening anecdote might establish a problem; a comparison might give readers another way to understand it; a final recommendation might suggest what to do about it. Follow changes in the argument, not just the order of paragraphs.

Titles framed as questions can invite a genuine debate, imply an answer or set up a playful provocation. An ending may answer the title directly, leave a challenge or narrow a large claim into an everyday action. Consider what the reader is asked to think or do by the end.

When images are present, read them with the argument. A photograph might illustrate the subject, lend weight to an account or complicate a humorous caption. Do not assume that every image creates sympathy or that visual features require a separate paragraph regardless of the guiding question.

## Useful vocabulary and common traps

- **Claim:** a statement the writer wants readers to accept.
- **Assumption:** a belief the argument relies on without fully establishing it.
- **Concession:** acceptance of a point that might seem to weaken the writer’s case.
- **Rebuttal:** a response that challenges an opposing claim or reason.
- **Irony:** a gap between a statement’s apparent meaning and what context invites us to understand.
- **Self-deprecation:** humor at the speaker’s or writer’s own expense.
- **Hyperbole:** deliberate exaggeration. Explain what is being enlarged and why.
- **Analogy:** a comparison used to explain or argue a point. Ask what the comparison makes easier to accept and where its limits lie.

Avoid debating the issue instead of analyzing the writing. You may identify an unsupported generalisation or uncertain statistic, but connect that observation to how the text presents its case. Your response is not a vote for or against the writer’s opinion.

Do not make ethos, pathos and logos your automatic paragraph headings. If emotion matters, name the emotion and show how it develops. If credibility matters, explain how it is established. If reasoning matters, examine how the evidence supports the conclusion. A number alone does not make an argument logical.

For further terms and examples, use the [analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference) and [analytical language bank](/resources/analytical-language).

## A practical reading method

1. Establish the issue, publication context and likely readers.
2. Put the writer’s position into your own words, allowing for irony or a delayed reveal.
3. Trace the argument: what does each stage add, qualify or change?
4. Name two or three specific attitudes and locate the words that establish them. Notice who or what each attitude targets.
5. Connect voice and reasoning. How does the manner of presenting a claim make it easier to accept, remember or question?
6. Build an interpretation that answers the guiding question. Select connected evidence and test it against a complication.

Return to [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d) for planning and writing the full response.

## Worked example

## Read the column as a whole

Alasdair McClintock’s “Should Netball Be Our National Sport?” appeared in the Sydney-based magazine *The Beast* on 1 May 2019. The supplied exam version is cataloged as November 2023, TZ2, Text 2. Its question asks: **How is tone used to shape the meaning of this text?**

The title raises a large question about national identity, but the column approaches it through familiar sporting complaints and jokes. It gradually makes an affectionate case for netball, then ends by encouraging readers to attend or watch games. It offers playful advocacy rather than a formal process for selecting a national sport.

The likely audience includes Australian readers familiar with sporting rivalries and local references. The commentary should explain those assumptions without claiming that every Australian shares the writer’s tastes. Read the whole short column first, then follow the selected passages beside each stage of the analysis.

The source layout remains available above the transcript. Its photograph shows a contested moment in a netball match; the accompanying caption reads “Great for the joints, by Liz Ellis.” The image gives the sporting topic a concrete setting, but the guiding question makes the development of voice our main focus. This walkthrough and model are original teaching material, not an official marked response.

## Set up an attack and reverse it

The opening strings together exaggerated complaints about other sports. The stretched “soooo” makes boredom sound like a performed whine, while the exclamations create the noisy energy of sporting rivalry. These are presented as things people say, not as a settled statement of the columnist’s own beliefs.

The question about anyone attacking netball’s “good name” prepares an exception. “Well, I think it’s about time someone did” appears to announce that the columnist will supply the missing attack. The isolated sentence delays the reversal just long enough to establish that expectation.

“Joking!” abruptly cancels it. The reader has briefly been led toward hostility, only to find a defender of the sport. This teasing movement makes the column’s affection entertaining rather than solemn. The writer’s refusal to insult netball also begins to establish its unusually protected status.

The follow-up exception for UFC undercuts the broad claim to love every sport. Preferring its participants to punch each other rather than him makes his objection comically self-protective. The voice invites readers into a casual conversation where qualifications arrive as jokes.

## Turn sporting rivalry into a family

Calling netball “the favourite child of the Aussie family” turns a public question into a familiar domestic relationship. Personification gives the sport an agreeable character: it is “genial,” lacks its siblings’ “hang-ups” and wants a “merry old time.” The analogy makes affection, rather than size or dominance, the reason for its special standing.

The aside “but not too good looking” gently punctures the praise. Netball should be attractive enough to like without becoming so perfect that it provokes resentment. This small qualification sustains an amused, affectionate tone and keeps the paragraph from sounding like an official promotional statement.

The family comparison also carries the opening’s structure forward. Other sports have already attracted criticism; now they become the more troublesome siblings against which netball appears uncomplicated. The paragraph therefore develops the argument through its tone of fond familiarity, not merely through a decorative metaphor.

## Make uncertainty part of the voice

The government website appears to offer a more factual basis for the claim. Yet the writer cannot confidently identify what its participation ranking measures: a state, the country or children in a particular age range. That accumulating uncertainty interrupts the expectation that an official statistic will settle the question.

“Smarter people than me” turns the joke against the writer. His confession that the page gave him “a headache” and made him “slightly angry” presents a fallible, impatient reader rather than an expert researcher. Readers who recognize the frustration may feel closer to him, even as the admission weakens the statistic’s value as evidence.

Keep those effects distinct. The passage can build rapport without establishing factual authority. Do not state that netball is definitely Australia’s sixth most popular sport on the basis of a sentence that openly leaves the population uncertain.

This is also more than a random digression. It prepares the next paragraph’s move away from numerical ranking toward affection as the basis of national importance.

## Replace ranking with shared affection

“But, while the numbers may not fully add up” concedes a weakness in the quantitative case. The column then shifts the standard: netball holds “the dearest spot in our national hearts.” What matters is now its supposed place in collective affection, rather than a verified participation total.

The short parallel claims “We all like it. We all smile when we see it” sound warmly certain after the preceding confusion. Inclusive “we” invites readers into a shared response, and “all” makes agreement seem universal. That is the voice’s persuasive claim; the column has not surveyed everyone.

The national team’s success adds pride to affection. “They win a lot of things” gives achievement an understated, conversational expression. The suggestion that such victories are now “like hens’ teeth” carries a wry implication that successes elsewhere have become scarce. We need not identify an unstated sporting scandal or tournament to explain the contrast.

Across these paragraphs, the writer moves from uncertain research to confident communal feeling. The humor makes that change of grounds seem relaxed, while the repeated collective language encourages readers to accept netball as something “we” value together.

## End with an ordinary invitation

The ending turns a grand question about a national sport into a modest action: “You should get down to a few games.” The colloquial invitation fits the companionable voice already established. Readers can also watch on free-to-air television, so support appears accessible rather than demanding.

The description of the competition as “creatively named” is a small ironic jab at its straightforward sponsored title. It maintains the teasing voice even as the writer offers practical information. Admiration does not require him to stop making jokes.

“Channel Nine, to be precise” supplies a concrete detail after the earlier confusion about statistics. Finally, “You know, like most major sports” makes recognition the closing issue. Its conversational reminder implies that netball already belongs alongside the sports readers take seriously.

The column never needs to establish an official national designation. Its movement from mock attack to affection and invitation encourages readers to give netball attention and support. Tone makes that advocacy feel like a recommendation from a witty fellow spectator.

## Build an analytical response

### A possible thesis

McClintock uses teasing reversals and jokes at his own expense to make his praise of netball feel like a friendly conversation. The column moves from mock hostility to shared affection and an invitation to attend or watch, encouraging readers to give the sport more recognition.

### Choose a manageable argument

A response could first trace how the opening establishes a teasing supporter, then examine how the uncertain statistic gives way to collective affection, and finally explain the closing invitation. The family comparison can support the first or second idea. This is one possible organization; you do not need a separate paragraph for every tonal label or every paragraph of the source.

### Model paragraph

McClintock shifts from uncertain research to shared affection to make his case for netball. A government website initially seems to offer reliable support, but he cannot work out which group its ranking describes. The growing list of possibilities makes his confusion comic. “Smarter people than me” directs the joke at himself, creating an approachable voice rather than an expert one. He then describes netball as holding “the dearest spot in our national hearts.” This changes the basis of his argument from participation figures to affection. “We all like it. We all smile when we see it” makes that affection sound widely shared. The shift invites readers to value netball for its place in community life, even though the statistic has not been established.

The paragraph follows a change in the argument and connects it to a change in tone. It explains what the self-deprecation achieves without confusing an approachable persona with reliable research. Its quotations are selective; the analysis does not need to retell the entire column.

## Practice and transfer

Write a paragraph on the opening reversal. Connect the threat to attack netball, “Joking!” and the UFC aside. Explain what kind of relationship with readers this sequence establishes and how it prepares the later praise.

Alternatively, connect the affectionate family comparison with the final invitation. How does making netball seem likeable prepare readers to give it attention?

Before exporting, check whether each tone word identifies an attitude toward something specific. Replace “the tone is humorous” with an explanation of what is being joked about and what that joke allows the writer to say.

For another opinion piece, trace the particular relationship between voice and argument. Anger may make an issue urgent; a measured concession may make a proposal seem fair. Do not assume that another columnist’s jokes or pronouns serve the same purpose as these.

items.summary: Read speaker, occasion, audience and language shaped for listening, with a worked example of Helen Clark’s tribute to Sir Edmund Hillary.
items.body:
## What makes a speech

A speech addresses an audience on a particular occasion. It may explain, persuade, celebrate, commemorate, welcome, protest or call people to act. Even when prepared in writing, it is usually shaped for listeners who encounter its ideas as they unfold.

Begin with the situation: who is speaking, to whom, where and why? A graduation address, a parliamentary speech and a funeral tribute ask different things of their audiences. The same technique can do different work in each. Repetition might reinforce a demand, make a complex idea easier to follow or give grief a shared expression.

A transcript gives us the words and their arrangement. It does not automatically tell us how loudly the speaker spoke, where they paused or how the audience reacted. Analyze the evidence supplied. You can explain how short clauses create opportunities for emphasis without claiming to have heard a particular delivery.

## Purposes and overlapping forms

- **Political or campaigning speeches** seek support for a position, policy, candidate or cause. Examine how they define a problem and make a response seem necessary.
- **Ceremonial speeches** mark an occasion, honour people or affirm values. Awards addresses, welcomes and tributes may strengthen a group’s sense of who it is.
- **Eulogies** honour someone who has died. They can acknowledge loss, select memories, offer consolation and identify a legacy. Praise and mourning may work together.
- **Informative talks or lectures** guide listeners through knowledge or an explanation. Their examples, signposting and definitions help an audience follow a developing account.
- **Motivational or commencement addresses** often connect an experience or lesson with the audience’s future choices. Ask how the speaker makes that lesson relevant to these listeners.
- **Protest speeches** voice grievances, challenge authority and build solidarity. They may address supporters and opponents at the same time.

These purposes overlap. A tribute may encourage action, and a political speech may commemorate a shared history. Do not assume every speech needs a controversial position, an opponent or an explicit call to action.

## Speaker, occasion and audience

Establish the speaker’s role from the supplied context. A head of government may speak as a national representative; a family member may speak from personal knowledge. A speaker can move between public authority and personal memory within the same address.

Distinguish the immediate listeners from possible wider audiences. A speech may be delivered in a room, broadcast or published afterward. Only claim a broadcast or setting when the source establishes it. A transcript published in a newspaper can reach readers beyond the original occasion, but its “today” and “here” still refer to the speaking situation.

Look closely at “I,” “we,” “you” and “they.” Who belongs to each group? Inclusive “we” can join people in a shared value or experience, while also assuming agreement that may not be universal. An audience should not become an undifferentiated “everyone” in your analysis.

Consider what listeners are likely to know and what they need explained. A familiar name may establish common ground; a short anecdote may give an abstract value a recognizable form. Connect these choices to the particular occasion and audience.

## Follow the movement of the speech

Map what changes as the speech develops. Does it move from a specific memory to a wider claim, from a problem to a proposal, or from mourning to a sense of continuing responsibility? Paragraph boundaries help, but a speech can return to an earlier idea instead of progressing through a simple timeline.

Notice the transitions that rank ideas. “But above all” does more than introduce another point: it tells listeners which consideration matters most. A return to the opening image can give an ending coherence; a final instruction can ask listeners to act on what they have considered.

Read the ending in relation to the whole. What are listeners invited to carry away: a decision, a changed attitude, a shared memory or a commitment? Avoid treating the final sentence as a detachable slogan.

## Language shaped for listening

**Repetition and parallel structure** can make a sequence easy to follow and accumulate emphasis. Examine what changes inside the repeated pattern. A series of similar openings may lead toward a final quality or claim that the speaker gives special weight.

**Sentence length and punctuation** shape the written rhythm. Short clauses may give a judgment force; a longer list may build a sense of scale. Punctuation suggests possible phrasing, but does not prove the precise timing of a performance.

**Direct address, questions and inclusive language** establish a relationship with listeners. A question might invite reflection or guide an audience toward an answer. “We” may express solidarity, responsibility or institutional authority. Name the function it serves here.

**Images, comparisons and examples** make ideas easier to picture and remember. Ask how a speaker turns an abstract value such as courage or service into something concrete. A historical example can support a claim without proving that every later situation is equivalent.

**Register and tone** help a speech suit its occasion. Formal naming may show respect; a familiar nickname may express affection. Humor within a solemn speech need not undermine its seriousness: it may help an audience remember a person’s character. Identify the particular shift and its purpose.

## Credibility, emotion and reasoning

A speaker may arrive with authority from their office, expertise or relationship to the subject. They can also build credibility through the speech: recognizing another person’s loss, acknowledging limits or giving precise examples may help listeners trust their judgment.

When analyzing emotion, name it. Pride, protective concern, gratitude and grief are different responses, and a speech may connect or move between them. Explain how the language invites that response rather than assuming all listeners actually felt it.

Reasoning also takes different forms. A policy speech may connect evidence to a proposed solution; a tribute may select actions that illustrate a person’s values. Do not force either into a fixed ethos–pathos–logos paragraph plan. Appeal labels are useful only when they help explain how this speech works.

Use the [analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference) and [analytical language bank](/resources/analytical-language) for further terms and examples. Particularly useful terms include **anaphora** (repetition at successive openings), **parallelism** (similar grammatical structures), **antithesis** (sharply contrasted ideas) and **allusion** (a reference that draws on shared knowledge).

## A practical reading method

1. Establish the speaker, occasion, audience and available source: transcript, recording or both.
2. State what the speech seeks to do on this occasion. Go beyond a general verb such as “persuade.”
3. Trace its movement, including returns, contrasts and changes in scale or tone.
4. Identify repeated language and examine how it develops. Ask who is included in collective pronouns.
5. Connect precise choices to an audience response and the speech’s larger purpose.
6. Test your interpretation against a qualification. Does praise acknowledge limits? Does a collective identity include people with different experiences?

Avoid a biography of the speaker or subject that displaces close reading. Keep performance claims tied to the evidence supplied. For planning the complete response, return to [Language & Literature Paper 1](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d).

## Worked example

## Read the tribute as a whole

Helen Clark speaks as Prime Minister of New Zealand at Sir Edmund Hillary’s state funeral. The supplied source describes an adaptation of her tribute published in the *New Zealand Herald* on 22 January 2008. It appears in the catalog as November 2020, Text C, from the older comparative Paper 1.

For this standalone reading, use our **practice question: How does Clark shape the audience’s response to Hillary’s life and legacy?** This is an original teaching question, not a question printed beside the extract in the examination.

The tribute connects Hillary’s extraordinary achievements with qualities listeners can value and practice. It invites pride and grief, but ends by making compassion an attainable legacy. Read both source pages before focusing on individual passages. The transcript follows the supplied adaptation; the [official government transcript](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/speech/eulogy-sir-edmund-hillary) is linked for context and includes material omitted here.

This is a reading of the words, not a reconstruction of the performance. Repetition and short sentences allow us to discuss emphasis and rhythm without inventing Clark’s gestures, pauses or the audience’s reactions. The walkthrough and model writing are original teaching material.

## Make achievement reveal character

The opening places “a young New Zealander” on Everest alongside Tenzing Norgay before naming Hillary. That movement gives the familiar hero a national and human starting point. His later fame grows from the young person introduced in the first sentence.

The repeated “He went” builds a sequence of reasons to admire the ascent. Clark identifies the unprecedented height, the limitations of “1950s, not 21st Century, technology,” and the skills developed in several places. The repeated opening gives listeners a stable pattern while the details accumulate.

“But above all” ranks attitude above those circumstances and skills. The further repetition of “with” gives goal, courage and determination a cumulative weight. The passage does more than list what happened: it directs attention toward what the achievement reveals about Hillary.

The following sentence connects that determination with pragmatism and humility. This matters because the tribute will later ask listeners to value qualities they can share, not simply marvel at a feat few could repeat. Tenzing is named at the opening and again later; do not turn the tribute into a claim that Hillary climbed alone.

## Bring private loss into national mourning

“Today” moves the speech from the remembered ascent to the funeral occasion. Clark names Lady Hillary, Peter and Sarah and acknowledges that their loss is “personal and profound.” The repeated language of sharing respects the family’s particular grief while recognizing a wider farewell.

“We mourn as a nation” then enlarges the group. The reason given is intimate: “we are saying goodbye to a friend.” Calling Hillary part of the “New Zealand family” extends the language of kinship beyond his actual relatives. The nation becomes a community joined by affection and loss.

Clark makes room for different degrees of personal connection: “a lot, a little, or not at all.” This sequence includes listeners who never met Hillary without claiming that their grief is identical to his family’s. Her initial acknowledgment of the family helps sustain that distinction.

The movement across parents, grandparents and “today’s children” extends belonging through time. Clark’s brief “My” places her own family inside the collective memory. Admiration becomes gratitude for having lived alongside a “living legend,” giving the mourning a sense of shared privilege as well as loss.

## Keep the hero recognizably human

Clark returns to Everest and enlarges the challenge: it had defeated fifteen expeditions and seemed beyond “mere mortals.” This elevated description makes success look exceptional. Yet the next paragraph identifies Hillary as “a beekeeper from New Zealand” alongside Tenzing, a Sherpa from Nepal.

That contrast brings extraordinary achievement into contact with ordinary identity. The modest occupation prevents the hero from appearing wholly separate from everyday life. The repeated partnership also gives both climbers a place in the historical achievement.

The later tractor detail performs related work. “In Kiwi style” associates a practical, unglamorous vehicle with the national character Clark is celebrating. The concise sentence can introduce warmth into the account of polar exploration. We can explain that tonal possibility without asserting that the audience laughed.

These details support the tribute’s combination of grandeur and familiarity. Hillary can be a world figure and “Sir Ed,” someone the audience is invited to recognize as one of its own.

## Make service the lasting achievement

The account moves from exploration to the Himalayan Trust, education, health services, patronage and diplomacy. These details widen the meaning of achievement. Hillary’s significance includes what his status allowed him to do for other people, in Nepal as well as New Zealand.

“Living legacy” is especially important in a funeral tribute. Although the person has died, the work described continues to matter. The phrase directs attention toward a lasting benefit rather than only a completed adventure. The examples give substance to the later praise of service.

Clark then contrasts Hillary’s own account of “modest abilities” with “a colossus.” The enlarged image honors his stature while preserving humility as part of his character. The short statements that follow—“He was our hero. He brought fame to our country”—give public achievement a firm, memorable shape.

The second “But above all” changes the emphasis again. “We admired his achievements” becomes “we loved Sir Ed for what he represented.” The contrast moves from accomplishment and reputation to attachment and values: determination, humility, fairness and service. It does not reject his fame; it explains why the tribute regards his character as more important.

## Give the audience an attainable legacy

The closing comparison makes that priority practical. Clark concedes that listeners may not match Hillary’s “abilities or strength,” but insists that “we can all strive” to match his humanity and compassion. The repeated “match” holds the two possibilities together while distinguishing what is exceptional from what is open to everyone.

“Strive” asks for effort rather than promising that every listener will instantly equal him. This makes the invitation both inclusive and demanding. The tribute turns a life to admire into a standard for future conduct without asking the audience to become mountaineers.

“His values were strong; they are timeless; and they will endure” moves through past, present and future. Its parallel clauses give the ending a sense of continuation: death does not end the relevance of those values. The final wish that Hillary “rest in peace” returns to the immediate purpose of a funeral farewell.

The closing therefore holds consolation and responsibility together. Listeners can honour the loss by carrying something forward, while the speaker still gives the dead person a respectful leave-taking.

## Build an analytical response

### A possible thesis

Clark presents Hillary as an extraordinary achiever whose humility and service made him a familiar national figure. Her tribute connects pride with shared loss, then encourages listeners to continue his example through compassion rather than feats of physical achievement.

### Choose a manageable argument

A response could examine how achievement is made to reveal character, how family language creates shared mourning, and how the ending makes that character an example for listeners. Select evidence that develops those ideas; you do not need to retell every event in the tribute. This is one possible structure, not a requirement to write three paragraphs or divide the speech into three appeals.

### Model paragraph

Clark makes Hillary’s example something listeners can try to follow. She first acknowledges that “we may not be able to match” his abilities or strength. She then turns to what “we can all strive to match”: his humanity and compassion. Repeating “match” connects two kinds of achievement. Physical feats may be beyond the listeners, but care for others is presented as possible for everyone. “We” includes Clark in this effort, while “all” extends it across the audience. The word “strive” also suggests that following his example will take work. The tribute gives mourners a way to honor Hillary through their own actions, as well as admire what he achieved.

The paragraph follows one contrast and explains its development. It connects grammar, word choice and audience without making unsupported claims about delivery or treating every listener’s response as certain.

## Practice and transfer

Write a paragraph connecting the acknowledgment of Hillary’s actual family with the later “New Zealand family.” Explain how Clark widens the circle of mourning while recognizing different relationships to him.

Alternatively, compare the two uses of “But above all.” What does each give priority to, and how do they prepare the final invitation to emulate Hillary’s compassion?

Before exporting, check that each claim about an audience response is supported by the language. If you describe a pause, gesture, applause or change in volume, ask whether the supplied source actually records it.

For another speech, begin again with its occasion. A campaign address may seek a decision, a lecture may guide understanding, and a protest may build solidarity. Transfer the method of tracing voice, structure and audience; do not import this tribute’s movement from mourning to legacy.
