items.summary: Read news, features and explainers through their angle, sources, structure and language, with a separate Lensa AI worked example.
items.body:
## What articles do

Articles help readers understand events, people, discoveries and issues. They appear in newspapers, magazines and online publications. Some report what has happened; others explore why it matters or explain something readers find confusing. An article can inform and influence at the same time: its selection of facts, voices and examples gives readers a particular way of seeing the subject.

Start with what this article is trying to help its readers understand. “It informs the reader” is only a starting point. What becomes clearer, more urgent, more surprising or more questionable by the end?

## News, features and explainers

**News reports** usually focus on a recent event or development. An opening may give the most important information first, followed by supporting details, quotations and background. This is often called the **inverted pyramid**. Check the actual order rather than assuming every report follows it.

**Features** explore a subject in more depth, often through people, scenes or a sustained angle. A profile may introduce someone through a revealing moment before widening into their life and work. A feature about a social issue may move between one person's experience and a wider pattern. Ask what the individual story helps readers see—and what it cannot establish on its own.

**Explainers** make a difficult or disputed subject more understandable. Definitions, comparisons, question headings and everyday examples can guide readers through unfamiliar ideas. Explanation still involves choices: the writer decides which questions matter and what counts as a useful answer.

These forms overlap. A feature can report new information; an explainer can express a judgment. An **opinion article** primarily develops a viewpoint, though it may also explain and report. Use the separate [Opinion/commentary guide](/courses/language-literature/text-types/9860d817-e8b4-4a15-b499-b0df6b780f28) when that is the main task. A publication's name does not determine the genre of everything it publishes.

## Readers, purpose and angle

Consider what the article assumes readers already know, what it explains and why those readers might care. Specialist vocabulary without explanation can suggest a knowledgeable readership; definitions and familiar comparisons may welcome readers new to a topic. Support these inferences with details rather than assigning an exact age or income without evidence.

The **angle** is the aspect of the subject the article focuses on. An article about transport might center on commuters' costs, environmental consequences or the experience of disabled passengers. Each angle directs attention differently, even when the articles concern the same policy.

Distinguish the subject from the developing message. “This is about public transport” identifies a topic. “The article makes a policy debate concrete through passengers' daily difficulties” begins to explain a choice and its purpose.

## Structure and the reading path

Read the headline with the opening, then trace what each section adds. A headline may announce, question, surprise or challenge an assumption. A **standfirst** is a short summary below the headline; an opening paragraph is sometimes called the **lead** or **lede**. Name these features when they help explain how the article prepares readers.

An article may move from event to background, problem to explanation, individual to wider pattern, or competing claims to a qualified judgment. Subheadings can make that movement visible. Notice where a writer pauses to define a term, introduces a different voice or changes the scale of the discussion.

The ending can resolve an opening question, return to a person or image, or leave readers with an unresolved consequence. Explain how that ending changes or completes what came before. Avoid treating structure as a list of paragraph summaries.

## Evidence, sources and credibility

Ask whose knowledge the article draws on. Named witnesses, researchers, organizations, documents and statistics can support different kinds of claim. A witness can describe an experience without representing everyone; an expert's relevant knowledge matters more than the title alone.

**Attribution** tells readers where information or a judgment comes from. Keep the writer's words distinct from a quoted speaker's: a forceful quotation may be selected to introduce a disagreement rather than endorse its position. Notice which voices receive space, where they appear and whether their claims are tested or qualified. An absent perspective may limit the account, but absence alone does not prove deliberate deception.

Credibility can develop through clear explanation, precise sourcing and an honest acknowledgment of limits. A number is not automatically convincing: what is counted, what comparison is made and what conclusion follows? Likewise, an emotional personal story can make a consequence vivid without proving how common it is.

## Language, images and tone

Examine how word choice makes the topic manageable and meaningful. Technical terms can provide precision; definitions and analogies can make them accessible. A conversational aside may reduce distance between writer and reader. Evaluative words can suggest approval, doubt or urgency even in an article whose main purpose is to explain.

A metaphor can clarify one aspect of a subject while encouraging a particular judgment about it. Calling a development a “breakthrough” differs from calling it an “invasion”. Explain the association the wording introduces and how the surrounding passage supports or qualifies it. Do not stop at naming the device.

Where images, captions, pull quotations or graphics are supplied, read them alongside the words. A photograph may personalise an issue; its caption may redirect attention toward a wider problem. A graph can support a comparison, but its scale and labels matter. Analyze the layout you can actually see. A printed exam extract does not establish the original website's scrolling behavior, links or interactive features.

## A practical reading method

1. Establish the subject, publication context and likely reader. Identify whether the main work is reporting, exploring, explaining or arguing.
2. Put the central question or angle into your own words. Track how the opening prepares it and how the ending leaves it.
3. Follow two or three important movements in the article. Mark changes in scale, source, tone or degree of certainty.
4. Select precise evidence across language, structure and any supplied visuals. Explain how the choices work together rather than building a device checklist.
5. Form a claim about the understanding the article develops. Test it against a detail that complicates your first reading.

Use the [analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference) for terminology and [analytical language](/resources/analytical-language) to express relationships clearly. Your explanation of a choice matters more than the number of terms you use.

For planning and organizing a timed response, use the [Paper 1 guide](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d).

## Worked example

## Read the article as a whole

Brendan Paul Murphy's article appeared in The Conversation in December 2022 and is supplied here in its November 2024 exam version. Its immediate subject is Lensa, an app that generates stylised portraits. Its larger question is how readers should understand the relationship between an appealing new technology and the artists whose work helps make it possible.

The supplied question asks: **How and to what effect is figurative language used in shaping the meaning of this text?** Keep that focus while reading the whole article. Murphy does more than decorate a technical explanation: familiar images help readers understand the technology and consider its consequences.

Trace the movement from public excitement and artistic alarm, through explanation, to an uncertain future. The article challenges the label of theft while retaining concern about disruption. Its technical and legal statements belong to its 2022 context; this reading examines how those statements are presented, rather than treating them as current advice.

## Begin with a qualified correction

The headline opens with the direct answer “No”, as if replying to a question already circulating among readers. Yet “technically” limits that correction, while “but” introduces consequences that the correction does not settle. The colloquial “majorly shake up” makes disruption sound both substantial and easy to grasp. Before the body begins, readers are asked to separate a legal label from wider effects.

Look at the supplied image and caption as a pair. The vividly colored, polished portrait shows the kind of visual appeal that makes the technology attractive. Its caption turns attention toward artists' uncertain future and the possibility that copyright law may need to “catch up”. That personification presents law as lagging behind a moving technology. The image demonstrates appeal; the caption prevents appeal from becoming the whole story.

This is useful context for the question about figurative language. Keep the main argument focused on the wording rather than drifting into a separate essay on portrait color.

## Make excitement and alarm share an image

In the opening, the technology has “left the labs” and begun “colonising our visual culture”. The movement takes it from a specialist setting into shared everyday life. “Colonising” suggests expansion and occupation, making that arrival more forceful than a neutral word such as “entering”. It does not by itself establish a complete historical comparison with colonialism.

The repeated fire image then divides the response. Lensa has “lit a fire” among influencers but “a different kind of fire” among artists. The first suggests excitement or enthusiasm; the second, in the context of recognized styles and compromised work, suggests anger and alarm. Reusing the image makes the groups' reactions directly comparable: the same development that attracts one group troubles another.

“Warning bells” extends the sense of danger, while “perhaps a bit of their soul” makes the perceived loss personal as well as commercial. Murphy attributes this feeling to artists, then asks “But has it?” The turn prepares his legal distinction without erasing the emotional stakes he has just established.

## Guide readers through an unfamiliar system

The question heading “If it’s not direct theft, what is it?” anticipates the gap left by the opening answer. The inclusive “us non-computer-scientists” places the explanation alongside readers who may feel uncertain. “Taking a couple of steps back” makes understanding sound like a manageable change of perspective.

The “black boxes” image acknowledges that the system's internal workings are difficult to see or understand. Later, “injects” presents the user's photographs as an input entering a system, while “capture” makes the preservation of recognizable features easier to imagine. These expressions give non-specialists ways to picture an abstract process. They are explanatory images, not literal accounts of what software does.

Notice the limits of this abridged version. Terms such as “latent diffusion” remain relatively compressed. You can explain how the article welcomes readers without claiming it fully teaches the underlying technology. The longer original includes material not present in the exam text; it is not evidence for this response.

## Separate legal explanation from human consequences

The distinction between borrowing “ideas” and taking “actual snippets” supports the article's account of why imitation of a style differs from copying a particular work. Naming the Australian Arts Law Centre gives that account an identifiable source. In your analysis, attribute the legal claim to the article rather than turning it into your own general ruling.

The heading “What about the artists?” returns to the group most affected. “Nonetheless” matters: the writer's preceding explanation does not make their difficulties disappear. “Immensely disruptive”, “extremely upsetting” and “ripped-off” restore the practical and emotional cost. The last expression recalls the opening accusation while distinguishing a feeling of exploitation from the legal category the writer has discussed.

The next “However” qualifies the threat in turn, arguing that a specific subject, context and the artist's personality still matter. Track this movement between explanation and concern. Calling the tone simply “neutral” would miss the writer's sympathy and evaluation; calling it simply “anti-AI” would miss the appeal and capabilities he also recognizes.

## End with change that cannot be reversed

The suggestion that artists might “borrow a page from the influencer’s handbook” makes adaptation sound like learning a practice from another group. “Borrow” also echoes the earlier description of AI borrowing ideas. Here, however, it refers to artists adopting promotional methods, not to the software's use of artwork.

The ending shifts from cautious possibilities—“may”, “early days”—to “one thing is for sure”. The familiar idiom “the genie is out of the bottle” presents the technology as a released power that cannot simply be contained again. Its force lies in that change from uncertainty about outcomes to confidence about lasting disruption.

The idiom does not prove that every consequence will be harmful or that regulation is impossible. It leaves readers with a sense that the issue will require a response. Read it alongside the headline: the opening corrects a label, while the ending insists the consequences remain.

## Build an analytical response

An argument can follow what the figurative language helps the article do: make the dispute vivid, make the system approachable, and present change as lasting. Those are connected functions, not a compulsory three-part plan.

**Possible thesis:** Murphy uses familiar images to explain AI image generation and the disagreement around it. These comparisons show both its appeal and artists’ concerns, while his discussion of copyright complicates the claim that the technology is simply theft.

**One achievable model paragraph:**

Murphy repeats the image of fire to show how differently influencers and artists respond to Lensa. The app has “lit a fire” among influencers, but “a different kind of fire” among artists. For influencers, the image suggests excitement about the portraits. For artists, the account of recognizable styles makes it suggest anger and alarm. The same image therefore links opposing reactions to the same technology. “Warning bells” adds to the sense of concern before Murphy questions whether the app has broken the law. This sequence lets readers understand the artists’ response without treating that response as legal proof of theft.

The paragraph develops one relationship, uses short quotations and follows their place in the article. It does not need a separate label for every phrase or a claim that all readers respond identically.

## Practice and transfer

Write a paragraph connecting “black boxes” with one other image from the explanation. What does each help a non-specialist reader picture? Where does the comparison simplify rather than fully explain the process?

Then return to the ending. Connect its final idiom with either “technically” in the headline or “Nonetheless” in the final section. Explain how those details complicate a claim that the article simply reassures readers about AI.

For transfer, choose another article from your practice texts. Identify its central question, one moment where it helps readers understand, and one where it encourages a judgment. These may be the same moment. Build your analysis from that relationship rather than searching for the same metaphors again.

items.title: Webpages
items.summary: Read purpose, layout, navigation and invitations to act, with a separate Redwoods Treewalk worked example.
items.body:
## What webpages do

A webpage is a setting for communication, not a single purpose. It might sell an experience, explain a public service, introduce an organization, share a personal account or ask for support. Start with what this particular page helps or encourages its visitors to do.

Words, images and routes through the content work together. Visitors may read closely, scan headings, compare options or leave through a link. A useful analysis explains how the page supports some of those actions and makes others less prominent. “It has buttons because it is a website” identifies a feature without explaining its role.

## Purpose and overlapping forms

A homepage often introduces an organization and directs visitors toward several areas. A campaign or product page may concentrate on one request. An information page may help visitors understand a process, while a service page may help them complete it. Do not assume every webpage is primarily selling something.

Webpages overlap with other forms. A blog post, charity appeal or news article can appear on a website. Read the writing through its purpose and form, then consider what its digital presentation adds. An article's argument still matters even when menus surround it; a booking page needs a different reading from a personal reflection.

The worked example here is a tourism webpage. Its commercial purpose gives us one way to apply the overview, not a template for every online text.

## Visitors and their questions

Consider why someone might arrive at the page. Are they discovering the organization, comparing options, checking a detail or ready to act? A page may serve several visitors at once. A short summary, detailed explanation and prominent action button can offer different routes without requiring everyone to read every word.

Use evidence to infer audience. Family prices suggest people planning visits with children; unexplained specialist vocabulary suggests prior knowledge. An attractive photograph alone does not establish an exact age group or income. Distinguish a likely reader from the person shown in an image.

Ask which practical questions the page answers and which it leaves for elsewhere. Clear details can support persuasion by making a proposal easier to consider. An invitation becomes more usable when readers can find the time, cost, eligibility or next step that matters to them.

## Layout and visual hierarchy

**Visual hierarchy** is the relative prominence given to elements through size, position, contrast and spacing. A large image and headline may establish the page's promise; smaller headings can organize the supporting detail. Explain what receives attention and why that emphasis matters.

The large introductory image is often called a **hero image**. It may demonstrate a product, show people taking part or create a mood. Read it with the nearby words: does the headline name what we see, make a broader claim, or give the image a particular meaning?

Content blocks can make a long page easier to scan. Repeated arrangements may help visitors compare options; a change in color or layout may mark a shift from description to practical information. Avoid treating a presumed eye movement, such as a fixed Z-pattern, as proof. Describe the visible relationships and the reading paths they make available.

## Navigation and invitations to act

Menus, links and buttons show possible next steps. **Navigation** helps visitors find areas of a site; a **call to action** invites a particular response, such as registering, donating, booking or learning more. Some elements do both.

Look at wording and placement. “Find out more” leaves room for investigation; “Book now” asks for a stronger commitment. Repeating an action at different points can serve visitors who are ready at different stages. A button's contrast may make it easy to locate, but visibility alone does not prove that visitors click it.

A screenshot shows an invitation to interact, not the interaction itself. You can analyze what a menu label or button offers without inventing its destination, a checkout process, an animation or a response to hovering. Features demonstrated on a live page can be discussed as observed behavior; features absent from the supplied extract cannot.

## Language, imagery and trust

Direct address can place visitors in an imagined situation. Imperatives may invite exploration or give instructions. Sensory description can make an experience feel immediate, while specific measurements or practical details can help readers assess it. Explain the relationship between those choices rather than separating the page into “emotional” and “logical” boxes.

Images can suggest what participation will look or feel like. Consider setting, scale, viewpoint, people, color and the relationship between image and copy. A bright image need not mean happiness; explain what the color helps establish in this context. Photographs can show an experience while still presenting a carefully selected view of it.

Logos, awards, testimonials and named sources can establish trust. Identify whose judgment is being invoked and what it supports. An award badge suggests recognition; it does not independently prove every claim on the page. Likewise, environmental language presents a particular relationship with nature, which should be examined rather than automatically accepted or dismissed.

## A practical reading method

1. Identify the page's main purpose and the questions likely visitors bring to it.
2. Read the opening image and headline together. What promise, problem or identity do they establish?
3. Trace the visible content blocks and routes. What can readers explore, compare or do next?
4. Connect precise words and visual details. Explain how they develop or qualify the opening impression.
5. Examine practical information and invitations to act. How does the page help visitors move from interest toward a decision?
6. Build an argument about the page as a whole. Keep claims about behavior within what the supplied source shows.

Use the [analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference) for useful terminology. For planning a timed response, use the [Paper 1 guide](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d).

## Worked example

## Read the page as an invitation

The supplied May 2025 TZ2 text presents an extract from the Redwoods Treewalk website, promoting a forest-canopy walking experience in Rotorua, New Zealand. Read both source pages before moving into the close-ups. The guiding question is: **How do text and image work together to promote an experience?**

The page offers more than a view of trees. It presents ways to enter the forest, imagine a distinctive visit and choose between day and night. The visible sequence moves from an opening promise and welcome to descriptions, prices and tickets. Navigation also lets visitors consider different routes rather than following one compulsory sequence.

Our analysis uses the supplied exam version. Its prices and layout are historical source details, not current visitor information. The current website is linked in the source notes, but additions there are not evidence for this reading.

## Put the visitor inside the promise

The opening photograph shows visitors on a suspended walkway looking upwards into the trees. Their presence provides a human scale and demonstrates participation: this is somewhere readers could enter, not merely admire from a distance. The bridge stretches into the forest, while the overlaid title identifies the attraction.

“A Must Do Activity In Rotorua” turns the scene into a recommendation. “Must” presents the visit as an essential part of a local itinerary. The large white lettering stands out against the dark green forest, joining that claim to the visible experience.

The award badge adds a different reason to consider the visit. Its “EXPERIENCE AWARD WINNER” wording gives the promotional claim an appearance of recognized quality. Explain the combination: the image offers a glimpse of participation, the headline recommends it, and the badge lends support. The visitors' expressions and posture suggest interest; they do not establish what every visitor will feel.

## Make the engineered walk belong to nature

“Welcome to our wonderland” presents arrival as an invitation into something special. “Majestic and magical” and “a walk to remember” promise a memorable experience rather than simply a route between platforms. The dark, starry background and silhouetted trees carry this atmosphere beyond the opening photograph.

At the same time, the description acknowledges the built structure: “eco-suspended bridges and platforms” are designed to “honour and accentuate” the environment. The wording presents engineering as a way to appreciate nature, rather than an interruption of it. The precise “75-metre-tall” trees make the scale concrete while the verbs tell readers how to value the intervention.

Do not treat the “eco-” label as independent proof of environmental impact. The analytical point is how the page makes an elevated, constructed walk feel compatible with care for the forest.

## Offer two versions of the experience

“Extraordinary by day, mesmerising by night” places the two options in a parallel sentence. Both receive positive descriptions; the choice is between kinds of appeal. The paired “DISCOVER THE DAY” and “UNCOVER THE NIGHT” buttons turn that distinction into visible routes for further exploration. Their verbs make finding information sound like discovery itself.

Compare the daytime and night-time panels using the source controls. In daylight, tall trunks and small figures emphasize scale, while “peaceful haven” and “gentle giants” make that scale seem welcoming. The trees become impressive companions rather than a threat. “Open your eyes” and “surround yourself” invite readers to imagine their own presence.

At night, blue illumination around the platform contrasts with warmer lights higher among the trees. “Enchanting. Magical. Mesmerising.” gives each promised quality its own short sentence. “Forest and fantasy come alive” interprets the lighting as transformation. The images show distinct appearances; the language gives each an atmosphere.

The result is a reason to consider both visits, not simply to choose the better photograph. That possibility becomes explicit in the later day-and-night price option.

## Connect wonder with practical reassurance

The daytime panel includes an average duration of “30–40 minutes” immediately after its sensory description. This makes the proposed visit easier to fit into a plan. It does not prove the walk is suitable for every visitor, but it answers a practical question that the promise of wonder leaves open.

The price panel organizes admission into adult, child and family categories. “Day OR Night / Day AND Night Combo” distinguishes two products, with paired prices for each paying category. The repeated dollar values should be read through those headings; they are not discounted and original prices. “Children under 5: FREE” makes one family consideration easy to find.

Beside the information, a photograph continues the experience: two visitors look upwards from a platform among the trees. This keeps the imagined visit present while readers assess its cost. The change to a warm red-brown information panel separates the practical details from the night-time scene above without abandoning forest imagery.

The numbers matter because of what they help readers decide, not because their presence automatically counts as “logos”.

## Keep the next step visible

“BUY TICKETS” appears in the opening navigation and again beneath the prices. The first gives ready visitors a direct invitation; the second offers that invitation after descriptions and costs. Readers who need more information also have “FIND OUT MORE” beneath the day and night descriptions.

These labels offer different levels of commitment. “Discover”, “uncover” and “find out” encourage investigation; “buy” names the commercial action plainly. The page can sustain an atmosphere of discovery while still making its business purpose clear.

White rectangular buttons contrast with the darker photographic and colored backgrounds, making the options easy to distinguish. We can analyze those visible invitations without claiming to have tested their destinations in the historical version. Nor can the extract tell us how many readers eventually booked.

## Build an analytical response

A response can trace how the page makes the visit imaginable, gives day and night distinct appeal, and helps readers turn interest into a practical decision. Connect words and images throughout, rather than writing one paragraph on all the language and another on all the photographs.

**Possible thesis:** The webpage combines photographs and language of wonder to help readers imagine taking part in the Treewalk. The day and night scenes offer different attractions, while practical information and repeated ticket invitations encourage readers to plan a visit.

**One achievable model paragraph:**

The daytime panel makes the forest seem impressive but welcoming. The small figures beside the tall trunks give readers a sense of the trees’ size. The phrase “gentle giants” then guides how that size is understood. “Giants” emphasizes the scale, while “gentle” suggests that visitors need not find it threatening. “Peaceful haven” develops this promise of calm. The invitations to “open your eyes” and “surround yourself” ask readers to imagine being there. Together, the photograph and wording offer a quiet experience within the forest, rather than just a view of large trees.

This paragraph develops one effect through several connected details. It does not need to claim that the page guarantees safety or that every reader wants the same experience.

## Practice and transfer

Compare the daytime and night-time panels. Choose one visual detail and one phrase from each, then write a paragraph explaining the different experiences they offer. Finish by connecting that contrast with the day-and-night ticket option.

Alternatively, examine the price panel with its adjacent photograph. Explain how practical information and the continuing image of participation work together. Avoid treating the numbers as persuasive without identifying the decision they support.

For transfer, choose a service or information webpage. Trace what readers can understand or do at each stage. Which parts of your method still apply when the purpose is helping someone complete a task rather than selling an experience?

items.title: Letters
items.summary: Read personal, formal and public letters through recipient, relationship, purpose and voice, with a separate Steinbeck worked example.
items.body:
## What letters do

A letter addresses someone. That relationship shapes what the writer explains, assumes, asks for and leaves unsaid. Letters can advise, thank, complain, apologise, persuade, remember or maintain a connection. Several purposes may operate together: a parent can offer guidance while also showing affection; a complainant can express frustration while seeking a practical remedy.

Begin with the situation behind the writing. Who is addressing whom, about what, and why now? Then ask what the writer wants the recipient to understand, feel or do. “The purpose is to communicate” is too general to explain this particular letter.

## Personal, formal and public letters

**Personal letters** often draw on shared memories, names and experiences. Their intimacy can appear in what does not need explaining as much as in affectionate wording. A personal letter can still be carefully structured, serious or persuasive; informality does not mean an absence of craft.

**Formal letters** may deal with applications, complaints, requests or official decisions. Titles, a clear account of events and a specific requested outcome can help establish the relationship. Courtesy may express respect, protect the writer's credibility or make a difficult request easier to receive. Identify its function in context rather than treating polite language as empty convention.

**Open letters** address a named person or group while inviting a wider public to read. The stated recipient may have power to act, while other readers are asked to witness, support or judge. **Letters to an editor** similarly enter a public discussion through an addressed form. Do not assume the editor is their only meaningful audience.

A private letter can also be published later. Distinguish its original recipient from its later readership. Publication changes who can read it; it does not prove that the writer originally composed every sentence for those later readers.

## Relationship and authority

Consider familiarity, distance and power. What gives the writer a basis for speaking: experience, responsibility, expertise, shared history or a formal position? The letter may establish that authority through its language rather than simply rely on an existing title.

Direct address makes the recipient present in the writing. “You” can reassure, challenge, accuse or invite; the pronoun has no automatic effect. Likewise, “we” might express solidarity, speak for an institution or place the recipient outside a group. Identify who is included and what the sentence asks of them.

Look for how the writer handles the recipient's independence. Advice may be offered as a possibility or delivered as an instruction. A complaint may insist on a right while leaving room for a reply. These choices shape the relationship as well as the immediate message.

## A conversation with an absent reply

Many letters form one part of an exchange. References such as “you asked”, “as we discussed” or “thank you for your letter” bring earlier communication into the present text. A writer may quote, paraphrase or interpret what the recipient has said, then answer an anticipated question or objection.

Be precise about the evidence. If the earlier letter is not supplied, we know it through this writer's account. Do not invent the recipient's exact wording, motives or reaction. The reply can make us feel that we are following a conversation without giving us both sides of it.

Shared knowledge may explain a brief reference to a name or event. Rather than automatically calling that reference unclear, consider how it reflects the original relationship. Later readers may need notes that the original recipient did not.

## Structure and letter conventions

Dates, places, salutations and sign-offs establish the circumstances and relationship where they are supplied. **Salutation** means the opening address, such as “Dear Thom”; **sign-off** refers to the closing formula and name. Explain their particular contribution instead of listing them as proof that the text is a letter.

Trace how the body develops. A letter might move from reassurance to advice, from an account of events to a request, or from shared memories to a difficult admission. A warm opening can prepare for criticism; a final instruction can sharpen an otherwise reflective text. Consider why those parts appear in that order.

Short paragraphs, a postscript or explicit markers such as “first” and “finally” can organize the response. They may also give an exchange an informal, unfolding quality. Avoid assuming that a printed transcription preserves the writer's handwriting, original spacing or every feature of the manuscript.

## Voice, tone and precise evidence

Choose language that describes the relationship accurately: affectionate, deferential, firm, conciliatory, teasing, disappointed or protective may be more useful than simply “positive” or “negative”. Track shifts. A writer can sound confident about a principle but tentative about what the recipient should do next.

Examine vocabulary, sentence shape, questions, commands, qualifications and figurative language together. A brief instruction may carry authority; a later qualification may soften or refine it. An anecdote can make advice concrete, establish shared experience or invite the recipient to see a situation differently.

Treat the voice on the page as something the letter constructs. Warm language supports a reading of an affectionate tone; it does not give complete knowledge of the writer's character or the whole relationship. Similarly, analyzing an argument does not require endorsing all its assumptions.

## A practical reading method

1. Establish writer, recipient, occasion and purpose from the supplied context.
2. Separate the original addressee from any wider or later readership.
3. Trace how the letter represents the exchange: what does it answer, assume or anticipate?
4. Follow changes in tone, authority and the action or understanding requested.
5. Select connected details from the opening, body and ending. Explain their contribution to the relationship and purpose.
6. Develop a claim about what the letter accomplishes through its particular way of addressing someone.

Use the [analysis reference](/resources/analysis-reference) for terminology and the [analytical language resource](/resources/analytical-language) to express those connections. The [Paper 1 guide](/courses/language-literature/assessment/c621c061-5e55-46a6-91b1-82f356b67a3d) supports planning a timed response.

## Worked example

## Read the letter as a reply

John Steinbeck writes to his son Thom from New York on 10 November 1958. The opening refers to a letter received that morning; the reply goes on to discuss Thom's feelings for Susan. The supplied text later appeared in *Steinbeck: A Life in Letters* and was used in the November 2013 comparative examination.

Our standalone practice question is: **How does Steinbeck combine reassurance and advice in addressing his son?** This is an original teaching question, not the question from that older examination.

Read the whole letter before selecting details. Its central movement is from taking Thom's feelings seriously to helping him decide how to act, then back to reassurance and a family welcome. We have Steinbeck's response, not Thom's earlier letter. References to what Thom said are evidence of how this reply presents the exchange.

## Take the recipient seriously

“Dear Thom” names a familiar individual. “We had your letter this morning” places the reply within an ongoing exchange, while “my point of view” presents Steinbeck's answer as a perspective. Elaine will have hers. He begins with a willingness to respond rather than claiming to be the only possible source of wisdom.

“First” introduces a clear reassurance: being in love is “about the best thing that can happen to anyone”. The instruction “Don’t let anyone make it small or light to you” then defends the importance of the feeling. The metaphors of size and weight suggest how someone might belittle it.

Later, “You say this is not puppy love” acknowledges a distinction Thom has apparently made. Steinbeck's “of course” accepts the seriousness of that feeling. The phrase does not give us Thom's full account, but it shows the father responding to the possibility that his son might feel dismissed.

## Give advice a moral distinction

“Second” turns from accepting love to distinguishing its forms. The first is “selfish, mean, grasping, egotistical”; the accumulating adjectives make it sound possessive and inward-looking. The alternative is an “outpouring”, suggesting generosity directed beyond the self. The contrast gives the advice a clear ethical basis.

Steinbeck develops this through opposing effects. One kind makes a person “sick and small and weak”; the other releases “strength, and courage and goodness” and even unexpected wisdom. The repeated conjunctions allow each quality to accumulate, making the contrast emphatic and easy to follow.

The distinction is not just between good and bad feelings. The explanation of respect moves beyond manners toward recognizing another person as “unique and valuable”. This directs Thom's attention from how strongly he feels to how he regards someone else. The father's authority develops through the values he explains, not merely through the fact that he is a parent.

## Respect his feelings while guiding his actions

“But I don’t think you were asking me what you feel” adjusts the direction of the reply. “You know better than anyone” gives Thom authority over his own experience. Steinbeck then defines a role for himself: helping with “what to do about it”. The emphatic “that I can tell you” makes him confident without claiming to know his son's feelings better than his son does.

The following instructions combine affirmation and responsibility. “Glory in it” encourages appreciation; “Try to live up to it” asks Thom to respond well. When Steinbeck advises expressing love, “only you must remember” qualifies the confident opening claim by asking him to consider another person's shyness.

That qualification matters. The advice asks Thom to communicate, but also to attend to the person receiving the words. The statement about what “Girls” know generalises by gender; analyze it as part of this father's assumptions and voice, rather than adopting it as a universal fact.

## Make room for uncertainty

“It sometimes happens” introduces the possibility that affection will not be returned without presenting rejection as inevitable. The general phrasing gives Steinbeck a way to discuss a potentially painful outcome without predicting Susan's feelings. “But” then separates that outcome from the value of Thom's own feeling.

This reassurance develops the earlier instruction not to let anyone make love seem “small”. It prepares Thom for uncertainty while continuing to take his experience seriously. The tone is protective, but it does not promise that he will receive the answer he wants.

A useful reading connects these moments rather than assigning a new technique to every paragraph. Across the letter, reassurance supports advice by making difficult possibilities discussable.

## Return advice to the family relationship

“Lastly, I know your feeling because I have it” grounds the advice in shared experience. Steinbeck presents himself as someone who still feels love, rather than an adult looking back on an emotion he has outgrown. “I’m glad you have it” makes that connection explicitly affectionate.

The welcome for Susan turns a general discussion into a practical family response. Repeated “glad” and “welcome” suggest acceptance. Elaine's involvement also returns to the opening acknowledgment of another perspective: “maybe she can give you more help than I can” limits the father's claim to authority.

The final instructions, “don’t worry” and “not to hurry”, offer calm rather than a detailed plan. “Nothing good gets away” has the compact, memorable form of an aphorism—a short statement presented as a general truth. Here it works as a father's reassuring conclusion, not a guarantee about every relationship. “Love” and the intimate “Fa” finally return the advice to the bond that makes this letter possible.

## Build an analytical response

A response might follow three connected movements: accepting the seriousness of the feeling, distinguishing responsible action, and ending with shared experience and welcome. Those movements give an argument direction without turning the letter into a list of devices.

**Possible thesis:** Steinbeck reassures Thom by respecting his understanding of his own feelings while offering advice about how to act. His direct instructions give the letter confidence, but his qualifications and affectionate ending keep the advice considerate and personal.

**One achievable model paragraph:**

Steinbeck gives parental advice without dismissing his son’s independence. He tells Thom, “You know better than anyone” what he feels. This accepts Thom’s knowledge of his own experience. The father then offers help with “what to do about it”, distinguishing the feeling from the action it might lead to. Later, his instruction to express love is limited by the need to consider the other person’s shyness. He gives Thom a direction, but also asks him to think about another person’s feelings. The advice therefore encourages judgment rather than simple obedience.

The paragraph makes one claim and develops it through connected evidence. It explains the relationship created by the wording instead of repeating that a father is giving advice.

## Practice and transfer

Write a paragraph connecting the opening reassurance with the discussion of unreturned affection. How does Steinbeck prepare Thom for a possible disappointment while preserving the value of his feelings?

Then test the claim that the letter is simply confident advice. Choose a qualification or acknowledgment of someone else's perspective. Explain what it adds to the father's voice, rather than treating it as a contradiction that invalidates your reading.

For transfer, read a formal or open letter. Identify what gives its writer authority and how it represents the recipient. What changes when the writer seeks an institutional decision or public support rather than a personal conversation?

items.title: Podcasts/interviews
items.summary: Read speaker roles, conversational language, framing and the development of ideas, with a separate Happiness Lab transcript example.
items.body:
## What podcasts and interviews do

Podcasts are a medium, while interviews are a way of organizing an exchange. A podcast may contain interviews, a single narrator, reporting, storytelling or a panel discussion. Interviews can also appear in print, on video or on the radio. Start with the form actually supplied rather than assuming every podcast is a question-and-answer conversation.

These texts can explain, investigate, entertain, persuade or introduce a person's experience. Often they do several things at once. Ask what listeners or readers are being helped to understand, and how the roles of the speakers shape that understanding.

## Speakers, audience and purpose

Identify who introduces the subject, who contributes knowledge or experience, and who the exchange addresses beyond the speakers themselves. An interviewer may ask questions that an audience could have asked, explain unfamiliar references or challenge an answer. A guest may speak as an expert, witness, participant or advocate.

Authority can be introduced through a title or established through clear explanations, relevant examples and acknowledgment of limits. Familiarity can matter too: a host who calls a guest a friend creates a different opening relationship from a host who presents a disputed claim for challenge. Neither arrangement guarantees accuracy or dishonesty.

Consider the audience's likely knowledge and interests. A specialist term followed by an everyday comparison suggests an effort to include less familiar listeners. Direct address can make an unseen audience feel involved in an exchange they cannot immediately answer.

## How the exchange develops

Follow what each contribution does in relation to the previous one. A question may invite a story, narrow the topic, test a claim or request clarification. A response may answer directly, qualify an assumption, change direction or avoid part of the question. These relationships are more useful than counting how often each speaker talks.

Not every transition takes the form of a question. A host can summarize a point, introduce a new example or make a statement that prepares the guest's next contribution. In an edited podcast, narration may connect recorded extracts. Describe the arrangement you can see without claiming it proves an uninterrupted live conversation.

A **turn** is one speaker's contribution before another takes over. Notice changes in the function or length of turns, but do not treat a longer turn as proof of dominance without considering its role. An extended answer may simply supply the example the program needs.

## Spoken language and the transcript

A transcript turns speech into writing. It may preserve repetitions, unfinished phrases, fillers and conversational expressions, or it may remove some of them. Read what is present. Repetition can clarify a point or suggest someone formulating an idea; it does not automatically prove confusion or lack of preparation.

Pronouns, brief asides, familiar comparisons and signposts such as “so” or “it turns out” can help listeners follow ideas as they unfold. Explain their local function. “You know” might invite shared understanding, while a repeated phrase may emphasize a qualification that the audience needs to retain.

Distinguish wording from delivery. Unless the source supplies audio or reliable annotations, you cannot establish volume, pace, laughter, pauses or vocal emotion. Punctuation in a transcript is not a complete performance record. Timestamp gaps may reflect omitted material rather than silence.

## Explanation, evidence and stories

Listen—or read—for how abstract ideas become understandable. Definitions, analogies, contrasts and everyday examples can connect unfamiliar concepts with the audience's experience. A story may make a consequence imaginable or show a principle in practice. Explain what it illustrates and how far that example can support a wider claim.

Research findings and numbers need the same care they would in an article. What comparison is being made? What does the speaker infer from it? A named institution may support credibility, but the excerpt may not supply enough detail to assess the underlying study. Distinguish what the speaker claims from what the extract independently demonstrates.

If a contribution encourages an emotional response, name the response and explain its construction. Concern about isolation, relief at a possible solution and curiosity about a surprising result are different effects. “It uses pathos” does not explain any of them.

## Framing and the available evidence

Titles, episode descriptions, introductory remarks and promotional images can prepare an audience's expectations. Read them alongside the exchange when they are supplied. They may identify a problem, promise useful knowledge or give a serious subject an approachable identity.

Selection matters. A transcript excerpt can place particular contributions together and leave others out. Track the sequence in front of you while acknowledging its limits. An omission does not automatically prove manipulation; it does mean that the extract cannot stand for every moment of the full conversation.

When audio is part of the supplied source, consider how voice, music, sound and editing work with the words. When you have only a transcript, build your analysis from its language, speaker roles, structure and visible framing. Do not invent a soundtrack or an audience reaction.

## A practical reading method

1. Identify the medium, speakers, audience and main purpose.
2. Read the title and introduction with the opening exchange. What expectations do they create?
3. Trace the movement of ideas and what each speaker contributes to it.
4. Select precise language, evidence and examples. Connect them with the understanding or response being developed.
5. Look for qualifications, challenges or changes in direction that complicate your first impression.
6. Build a claim about the exchange as a whole, keeping performance claims within the evidence supplied.

## Worked example

## Read the extract as a developing explanation

The supplied May 2023 TZ1 text is an extract from *The Happiness Lab*, hosted by Dr. Laurie Santos. It presents Santos with psychologist Jamil Zaki in the episode “The War For Kindness”. The guiding question asks: **How and to what effect is empathy presented in the text?**

The extract moves from social division and declining empathy toward personal benefits and the possibility of developing empathy through practice. It ends by preserving a choice: understanding another person does not require agreement or an obligation to engage.

Keep the two voices in view. Santos introduces, connects and reframes; Zaki supplies personal experience, explanation and a classroom example. Their contributions make empathy appear necessary, beneficial and learnable. The transcript jumps from 18:42 to 23:22, so we should not describe the entire selection as continuous speech or interpret that gap as a long pause.

## Frame the subject through expertise and familiarity

The episode title, “The War For Kindness”, presents kindness as something that meets resistance. The description contrasts belonging with its “darker side” and promises a response through empathy and difficult conversations. This framing prepares the audience for a problem-and-response structure before the first speaking turn.

The bright yellow-green program artwork and curved “HAPPINESS” lettering give the serious subject an approachable visual frame. They do not remove the conflict named by “War”. For this question, the contrast is useful context; the main analysis should still follow how empathy is developed in the speakers' words.

Santos introduces Zaki as “my friend” and a professor at Stanford, then describes his book as “important”. Personal familiarity and professional credentials work together: listeners are offered a trusted conversation with someone presented as knowledgeable. This establishes a basis for attention, rather than proving every later claim in advance.

## Make the problem immediate

Zaki begins with his own experience of writing about empathy while feeling that social life was becoming “crueler and less connected”. “I don’t know” and “I can’t quite put my finger on what it was” qualify his ability to identify a precise change. They make the account sound conversational without erasing the strength of his concern.

His fear of being a “Pollyanna” presents optimism as potentially naive in that setting. The contrasting “giant tire fire” makes hostility seem destructive and difficult to contain. The image expresses his perception; it is not a literal description of the culture.

Santos picks up the conflict through “war for kindness” and “an uphill battle”. She then supplies a numerical comparison: an average empathy score of about 4 out of 5 in 1979 and 3.5 in 2009. The figures give the decline a concrete form and extend the discussion beyond Zaki's personal impressions. The extract does not provide the study's methods, so explain the comparison's role without claiming it proves every cause or consequence of social division.

## Reverse the assumption of sacrifice

Santos connects disconnection with a lost “potential boost to our well-being”, preparing Zaki's next explanation. He first voices a familiar assumption: empathy is a “transfer” in which helping another person costs money, time or “emotional peace”. The concrete examples make the perceived cost easy to recognize.

“It turns out, though” signals a reversal. Caring for others becomes “one of the most important ways we can care for ourselves”. The repeated “care” connects the two sides of the supposed exchange. Rather than asking listeners only to sacrifice, the explanation gives them a personal reason to value empathy.

The examples move through friendship, marriage and seventh grade, bringing the idea into recognizable relationships. “Survive seventh grade, which is not easy” adds a lightly humorous acknowledgment of difficulty. We can discuss that wording without inventing laughter or vocal delivery. Also retain “tend to”: the speaker presents a pattern of association, not a guarantee that empathy will cure distress.

## Turn a value into something people can practice

At 23:22, Santos describes empathy as “like a skill”. This comparison changes the practical question from whether someone possesses a quality to how they might develop it. “Cultivate” suggests growth through attention, while “super hard assignment” keeps the register conversational and acknowledges effort.

Zaki then gives the skill a method. He contrasts “yelling”, “judging” and “debating” with curiosity about how people came to their opinions. The paired instructions—“Ask the other person” and “share with them”—make the exchange reciprocal. Each person can explain a history rather than merely defend a position.

The examples of difficult family conversations make the challenge concrete. Predicted “frustration or even tears” is followed by “better than expected”, presenting practice as capable of changing an anticipated outcome. This is an account of the students' experiences, not proof that every difficult conversation will end well. Its role is to make the proposed skill imaginable and worth considering.

## Preserve choice in the final appeal

The final paragraph separates understanding from agreement: the new discussion need not depend on agreeing “on every point”. Empathy is presented as appreciating a person across disagreement, rather than surrendering one's own position.

Zaki then limits the invitation. “No one should feel like they’re obligated”, “No one has to do this” and “It’s not anybody’s job” repeat the absence of compulsion. The insistence matters because the preceding examples involve painful or offensive views. The qualification acknowledges that the effort being encouraged has a personal cost.

“But when we do” returns to the possibility of connection while preserving that choice. People “on the other side” are presented as waiting for “a chance to be human”. The ending shifts attention from opposing camps to shared humanity. It completes an argument for empathy that recognizes difficulty, rather than simply demanding that everyone be kinder.

## Build an analytical response

Organize your response around how the presentation develops: empathy is under pressure, offers benefits beyond self-sacrifice, and can be practiced without becoming compulsory. Explain how the speakers contribute to those ideas rather than writing separate summaries of everything Santos and Zaki say.

**Possible thesis:** Santos and Zaki present empathy as a way to respond to social division that can also help the person practicing it. Their comparisons and examples show how it can be learned. The final qualification makes clear that this is an invitation, not a duty to engage in every situation.

**One achievable model paragraph:**

The speakers make empathy seem learnable by moving from a comparison to a practical example. Santos calls it “like a skill,” suggesting that people can develop it. Zaki then describes an assignment in which students ask how others formed their opinions and share their own stories. Both people take a turn at listening and explaining, so the activity gives listeners a method they can picture. The students expected “frustration or even tears,” but the conversations went “better than expected.” This contrast suggests that trying the activity may be worthwhile, without guaranteeing the same result for everyone. Santos introduces the idea, and Zaki shows what putting it into practice can involve.

This paragraph follows one development across two voices. Its claims remain proportionate to the example rather than treating a reported classroom outcome as a universal result.
